card: Foreign minister of a Dual Monarchy that has just lost its heir. Will you punish Serbia, or hold back?
intro: You are Count Leopold von Berchtold, foreign minister of Austria-Hungary. Since the Compromise of 1867, Austria and Hungary have formed a Dual Monarchy, two governments under one monarch; foreign affairs and the army are common to both, and at the top stands the eighty-three-year-old Emperor Franz Joseph. You chair the Joint Council of Ministers, but if the Hungarian prime minister, István Tisza, who controls the Hungarian parliament, turns against you, no decision will last long. Beside you are Conrad von Hötzendorf, Chief of the General Staff, who has argued for years for a preventive war on Serbia; your chef de cabinet, Count Hoyos; and Count Forgách, a hard-line section chief. Whatever you plan, you must first weigh how far your ally Germany will go with you.

AT-00.title: Conrad’s First Demand
AT-00.event: Over two days from the evening of 28 June, Serb homes and shops were attacked in Sarajevo and Zagreb, and two Serbs were killed in Sarajevo. Today, 29 June, is a public holiday, but the heads of the government and the army have hurried back to Vienna.
AT-00.scene: Yesterday the Archduke and his wife were assassinated in Sarajevo, and this morning the Emperor returned to Vienna from Bad Ischl. Conrad, Chief of the General Staff, heard the news at Karlstadt (Karlovac) in Croatia-Slavonia and came up on the night train; now, ahead of the 8 p.m. ministerial council, he has come to see you. Inside the Foreign Ministry there is already talk of war with Serbia, and a young diplomat, Andrian-Werburg, has written to Colonel Brosch, once head of the Archduke’s military chancellery, that “very valuable fruit for the Monarchy should ripen” from the Archduke’s blood. Since becoming foreign minister in 1912 you have turned down every demand to strike Serbia, all through the Balkan Wars, and in mid-June the Archduke invited you to Konopiště in Bohemia to discuss affairs of state.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff, his judgment on the assassination as set down in his memoirs)
voices.text: The murder in Sarajevo was the last link in a long chain. It was not the work of an individual fanatic, but the result of a well-organised attack; it was a declaration of war by Serbia on Austria-Hungary. It can only be answered by war.

voices.who: Franz Ferdinand (letter to you of 1 February 1913, gist)
voices.text: There is no reason to go to war with Serbia. Let the Slavs of the empire be treated fairly and live in contentment, and the separatist movements that look across the frontier will soon die away.

choices.text: Back Conrad: ask the Emperor tonight to mobilize against Serbia, and strike before Europe’s sympathy cools
choices.why: The sooner you strike, the less room the powers have to step in
choices.after: Conrad went straight back to the General Staff with a draft submission for the Emperor. But before you could even see the Emperor, word reached the Foreign Ministry that the German embassy still had no instructions from Berlin.

choices.text: Turn down Conrad’s call for immediate mobilization. Consult the Emperor, agree on a procedure with Germany, then deal with Serbia.
choices.why: Without German backing, Austria-Hungary cannot take on Russia
choices.after: You did not accept Conrad’s plan for an immediate attack. When you saw the Emperor the next day, the two of you agreed that Serbia must be dealt with firmly, but that a procedure had to be agreed on with Germany before any invasion. But on 1 July, when you told Tisza you meant to use Sarajevo as the occasion for a reckoning with Serbia, he at once sent the Emperor a memorandum opposing it.

choices.text: Take up the Archduke’s ideas: open trade talks with Serbia and begin by improving the lot of the empire’s South Slavs
choices.why: Easing discontent at home strikes nearer the root than war
choices.after: Conrad stormed out, asking whether you meant to talk trade before the Archduke was even buried. Everyone in Vienna knows that the Archduke held back war with Serbia while he lived, but few are left who will carry his ideas forward.

note.text: In June 1903 army officers murdered King Alexander Obrenović and his wife in the royal palace in Belgrade. The Obrenović dynasty, which had mostly sided with Austria, came to an end, and Peter I of the Karađorđević dynasty, close to Russia and France, took the throne. The officers who led the coup later formed the core of the secret society known as the Black Hand.

map.caption: The Balkan Wars (1912–1913) greatly enlarged Serbia, but Albanian independence blocked its way to the Adriatic.

pressure.title: A Reputation for Weakness
pressure.text: Ever since you turned down the demands for war during the Balkan Wars, you have been criticized as indecisive. When you sat down with the Archduke at Konopiště in mid-June, you still saw a way to come to terms with Serbia, but now that same Archduke has been shot dead by a young Serb. Back down again this time, and the army and the press will level the same charge even more loudly.

AT-01.title: The First Move After Sarajevo

telegram.text: Archduke and Duchess shot / both dead / assassin, a young Bosnian, arrested at the scene

AT-01.event: On 1 July Tisza, the Hungarian prime minister, sent the Emperor a memorandum. With no evidence that the Serbian government was involved, he warned, using Sarajevo as a pretext for punishment would be a fatal mistake.
AT-01.scene: The Foreign Ministry faces the Hofburg across a single square, and tomorrow, 3 July, the funeral mass for the Archduke and his wife will be held in the palace chapel. The court is still whispering about what rank to accord Duchess Sophie, the Archduke’s morganatic wife. You are a wealthy, elegant nobleman with a love of horse racing and art; since becoming foreign minister in 1912 you have turned down Conrad’s calls for war all through the Balkan Wars, and the hard-liners have called you indecisive for it. This time the mood is different: on 29 June Conrad came to demand immediate mobilization, and when he received you on 30 June the Emperor made it clear that Serbia could not be left as it was.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Serbia slipped away in 1908, in 1912 and again in 1913. If we trade notes once more, the army and every nation in the empire will conclude that Vienna has no will to fight. We must mobilize at once.

There is no proof that the Serbian government was an accomplice. Romania has already drifted away from the Triple Alliance, and Bulgaria is worn out by two wars. Draw the sword now and the empire will stand before the world as the aggressor.

choices.text: Take Conrad’s plan and ask for immediate mobilization. Strike Serbia before Europe’s sympathy over Sarajevo cools.
choices.why: Move while the cause is still fresh in Europe’s mind
choices.after: Conrad was delighted, but Bolfras, head of the Emperor’s military chancellery, hinted that the Emperor would not approve mobilization without knowing Germany’s mind. In Budapest, Tisza had already sent in his memorandum of objection.

choices.text: Follow Tisza’s memorandum and keep the sword sheathed. First send Serbia a note demanding a joint inquiry into the plot.
choices.why: Drawing the sword without evidence would brand the empire the aggressor
choices.after: Conrad was indignant: a note, before the Archduke’s blood was even dry? From the embassy in Berlin came a report that the German Foreign Office was beginning to doubt Austria’s resolve.

choices.text: Find out what Berlin wants first. Send Hoyos to Berlin with the Emperor’s letter and the memorandum on Balkan policy.
choices.why: You must know how far Germany will go before you act
choices.after: On the night of 4 July your chef de cabinet, Count Hoyos, boarded the night train to Berlin carrying a personal letter from Franz Joseph and the Matscheko memorandum, drafted before Sarajevo and revised afterward. The letter said that Serbia must be eliminated as a political power in the Balkans.

note.text: In September 1908 Berchtold’s estate, Buchlau Castle in Moravia, hosted a secret meeting between the Austrian foreign minister Aehrenthal and the Russian foreign minister Izvolsky. The Bosnian annexation crisis that followed (1908–1909) left Russia humiliated, and the resentment lasted into July 1914.

AT-02.place: Vienna, Foreign Ministry, Ballhausplatz (Joint Council of Ministers)
AT-02.title: Tisza Stands Alone

telegram.text: Ambassador Szögyény / lunch at Potsdam / Kaiser Wilhelm: Germany will stand faithfully by Austria even if Russia intervenes / action should not be delayed

AT-02.event: On 6 July Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg, with Under-Secretary Zimmermann, met Hoyos and Szögyény and formally confirmed the Kaiser’s promise. Historians call it the “blank check.” At the same meeting, though, Hoyos offered his private view that Serbia might be divided among its neighbors, which later drew a furious protest from Tisza.
AT-02.scene: Around the table sit the Austrian prime minister Stürgkh, the Hungarian prime minister Tisza, the joint finance minister Biliński, who runs Bosnia, and the war minister Krobatin; Conrad and Admiral Kailer of the navy come in when military questions are discussed. Hoyos, just back from Berlin, keeps the minutes. Today the Emperor leaves by special train for his summer villa at Bad Ischl. Foreign policy and war are joint affairs of the two states, but if Tisza, who commands the majority in the Hungarian parliament, turns against you, neither recruits nor money can be counted on.

voices.text: He would never consent to a surprise attack on Serbia without prior diplomatic action.
The Serb understands only force. A diplomatic success would make no impression at all in Bosnia.

choices.text: Side with the majority and set demands Serbia is bound to reject. Win Tisza over separately, through the Emperor.
choices.why: A purely diplomatic success will not settle the Serbian problem
choices.after: According to the minutes, everyone present except the Hungarian prime minister agreed: a purely diplomatic success, even one that humiliated Serbia, would be worthless, so demands should be set whose rejection was all but certain, opening the way to a radical solution by military action. The next day Tisza sent the Emperor a memorandum of his own, and on 9 July you went to Bad Ischl and read it aloud to him.

choices.text: Follow Tisza: first send stiff demands that Serbia can meet. Move to an ultimatum only if Serbia refuses.
choices.why: Build the case first, and Europe will side with the empire
choices.after: For the first time Tisza nodded. But Krobatin and Biliński had their dissent entered in the minutes, warning that the decision would signal weakness to the army and to Bosnia.

choices.text: Do not wait for Tisza. Go to Bad Ischl for the Emperor’s assent, even if it means replacing the Hungarian premier.
choices.why: Losing time is more dangerous than Hungary’s opposition
choices.after: The meeting broke up without a decision, and Tisza, stony-faced, took the train back to Budapest. You set off for Bad Ischl.

note.text: Count Hoyos’s maternal grandfather was Robert Whitehead, the English engineer who created the modern torpedo. Whitehead’s torpedo works at the Adriatic port of Fiume (today Rijeka in Croatia) was run together with the Hoyos family and sold torpedoes to navies around the world.

AT-02a.time: The day after the Joint Council
AT-02a.title: As If Nothing Were Happening
AT-02a.scene: The Joint Council of 7 July ended with Tisza alone in opposition, and today he is sending the Emperor a memorandum of his own. Since 4 July the Foreign Ministry has been gathering material to show Serbia’s guilt and refining the demands; inside the ministry the work is called the “war factory.” You read a daily digest of the press, and Hungarian papers such as the Pester Lloyd call day after day for a reckoning with Serbia. If the Chief of the General Staff and the war minister are also seen bustling about Vienna, Belgrade and St Petersburg will soon guess what Vienna intends.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: If the Chief of the General Staff goes on leave, preparations fall behind by just as much. The men on leave will not be back until late July, and operations against Serbia are possible only some two weeks after mobilization begins.

voices.who: Serbian government declaration of 31 March 1909 (the document the ultimatum invoked)
voices.text: Serbia recognises that the fait accompli regarding Bosnia has not affected her rights, and consequently she will conform to the decisions that the Powers may take in conformity with article 25 of the Treaty of Berlin. In deference to the advice of the Great Powers, Serbia undertakes to renounce from now onwards the attitude of protest and opposition which she has adopted with regard to the annexation since last autumn. She undertakes, moreover, to modify the direction of her policy with regard to Austria-Hungary and to live in future on good neighbourly terms with the latter.

choices.text: Do as Conrad wishes and put the corps on the southern frontier on alert. If it cannot be hidden, at least prepare early.
choices.why: Time to prepare is worth more than time spent hiding it
choices.after: Belgrade soon noticed the movements across the border, and the military attaché at the Russian embassy in Vienna reported the same to his government. Serbian newspapers answered the Viennese press with sharp articles of their own.

choices.text: Take Tisza’s advice and lead with the evidence. Compile the Sarajevo case file and send it to the powers before the ultimatum.
choices.why: Europe must see Serbia’s guilt before anything else
choices.after: London and Paris received Vienna’s material coldly. Some newspapers revived the Friedjung trial of 1909, when the Foreign Ministry in Vienna had been shamed by forged documents, and Belgrade dismissed the file as the record of an unfinished investigation.

choices.text: Urge Conrad and Krobatin to take their leave as planned, and quietly polish the text as if nothing were happening
choices.why: Surprise works only if the preparations stay hidden
choices.after: Conrad was taken aback by the suggestion, and the Emperor, too, wanted leave put off. Even so, from 12 July the military chiefs were away from Vienna, the Emperor stayed at Bad Ischl, and Germany’s Wilhelm II left as planned on his North Sea cruise.

note.text: In 1909 the historian Friedjung, relying on documents supplied by the Foreign Ministry, wrote that politicians of the Croat-Serb Coalition had taken money from Belgrade; at the libel trial the documents were shown to be forgeries. That same year 53 Serbs were tried for treason in Zagreb (Agram), and 31 were sentenced to between five and twelve years in prison, but in April 1910 an appeal court quashed the verdicts.

pressure.title: Forgách’s Past
pressure.text: Putting the evidence first means working through your section chief, Forgách. He was minister in Belgrade when the documents later exposed as forgeries were reaching the Foreign Ministry in Vienna in 1909, and over that affair he was moved to Dresden before returning in the autumn of 1913. Rauchensteiner considers the memory of the Friedjung trial one of the reasons Vienna’s case found so little credit in 1914.

AT-03.title: Wiesner’s Telegram and Tisza’s Terms

telegram.text: Wiesner / nothing to prove or even suggest Serbian government complicity in the plot, its preparation or the supply of weapons / but bombs came from Serbian army depot at Kragujevac, Serbian officials involved

AT-03.event: On the evening of 10 July Hartwig, the Russian minister to Serbia, collapsed with a heart attack and died while talking with Giesl at the Austrian legation in Belgrade. Rumors spread through Belgrade that Austria had poisoned him.
AT-03.scene: Tisza comes to your office. Over the past week he has been told that Berlin stands firmly behind Austria and that every delay costs German trust. But this Hungarian nobleman, a strict Calvinist, insists that he cannot agree to a war that would take Serbian land and add to the empire’s Slavs. Four days ago, for your part, you confided to the German ambassador, Tschirschky, that it would be a very unpleasant solution if Serbia accepted every demand.

voices.who: Wiesner (Foreign Ministry legal adviser, telegram of 13 July)
voices.text: There is nothing to prove or even to suppose that the Serbian government is an accessory to carrying out the assassination, or its preparation or the furnishing of weapons. On the contrary, there are reasons to regard this as altogether out of the question.

voices.who: István Tisza (Hungarian prime minister, memorandum of 8 July)
voices.text: We must for our part at the appropriate time and in the appropriate manner issue a declaration that we do not wish to destroy Serbia, still less to annex it.
A promise not to annex ties the empire’s own hands after the war. At the very least we must keep open the option of cutting Serbia down and handing parts of it to its neighbors.

choices.text: Follow Forgách and refuse to renounce annexation. Keep the option of shrinking Serbia and sharing it among its neighbors.
choices.why: You cannot throw away your postwar options in advance
choices.after: Tisza went back to Budapest without giving his consent, and only just before the meeting of 19 July did he reluctantly sign off on a formal renunciation of annexation. In St Petersburg the suspicion grew that Austria meant to wipe Serbia off the map.

choices.text: Accept Tisza’s terms: renounce annexation, and hold back the ultimatum until Poincaré has left Russia
choices.why: One promise is a cheap price for Hungary’s consent
choices.after: Tisza finally agreed, and that day Tschirschky reported to Berlin that the Hungarian premier now backed resolute action. It was decided not to send the ultimatum while the French president Poincaré was in St Petersburg, from 20 to 23 July. The soldiers on harvest leave would not be back with their units until late July in any case.

choices.text: Take Wiesner’s report seriously: lower the demands and propose an international inquiry with the powers taking part
choices.why: Demands built on thin evidence will not win Europe’s support
choices.after: Forgách walked out, asking sharply on his way why you had not read the second part of Wiesner’s telegram. In Berlin people began to say that Vienna was backing away again.

note.text: The second part of Wiesner’s telegram reported that the decision to carry out the assassination had been made in Belgrade and that Serbian officials had been involved. After the war, only the first part was usually quoted, and it was used as proof that Austria’s suspicions had been groundless.

AT-04.place: Vienna, Berchtold’s private residence (Joint Council of Ministers)
AT-04.title: The Wording of the Ultimatum
AT-04.clock: 4 days until the ultimatum is delivered
AT-04.event: Told that the ultimatum was being put off until after Poincaré’s visit, Kaiser Wilhelm wrote in the margin of the report: “What a pity!”
AT-04.scene: To avoid prying eyes, the meeting is held at the foreign minister’s private residence. The text was drafted by Baron Musulin, a diplomat from Croatia, with help from Forgách. Of its ten points, point 5 requires Serbia to accept the collaboration of Austro-Hungarian organs in suppressing the anti-Austrian movement inside Serbia, and point 6 requires Austro-Hungarian officials to take part in the investigation of those involved in the plot; the deadline is 48 hours. Those present remember 18 October 1913, when Vienna sent Serbia a unilateral ultimatum over Albania with an eight-day deadline and Serbia promised within two days to withdraw its troops.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: If the ultimatum is rejected, we mobilize immediately. Operations against Serbia can begin only some two weeks after mobilization starts. Diplomacy must not be given an opening before then.
Put a resolution in the minutes that no Serbian territory will be annexed. Only then can Hungary agree to this text.

choices.text: Rewrite the text so Serbia can comply, as Tisza first wanted: drop points 5 and 6 and extend the deadline to five days
choices.why: If Serbia accepts, you win without bloodshed
choices.after: As they left the room, Forgách and Conrad exchanged a few grim whispers. That night Ambassador Tschirschky telegraphed Berlin that Vienna was hesitating again.

choices.text: Go with a text built to be rejected: ten points, a 48-hour deadline, points 5 and 6 intact, no way out
choices.why: Serbia must be left no way to slip out of it
choices.after: The council set 23 July for delivery of the ultimatum and resolved that, apart from frontier adjustments needed for strategic reasons, no Serbian territory would be annexed. But you did not rule out shrinking Serbia by handing parts of it to Bulgaria, Greece and Albania. When Wilhelm later heard of the renunciation of annexation, he wrote beside the passage: “Feeble!”

note.text: The ultimatum required the Serbian government to publish on the front page of its official journal a declaration condemning anti-Austrian propaganda, and to announce the same to the army in an order of the day from the King. Dictating to an independent government the very words it was to publish was an almost unprecedented demand.

AT-05.title: 6 p.m.
AT-05.clock: About 20 hours until the ultimatum is delivered

telegram.text: Szögyény / final text handed to State Secretary Jagow / no German objections / French president’s departure expected about an hour late

AT-05.scene: The French president Poincaré and Prime Minister Viviani have been in St Petersburg since 20 July and sail from Kronstadt tomorrow night aboard a warship. You had planned to deliver the ultimatum at 5 p.m. on 23 July, so that by the time the news broke the president would already be at sea and the French and Russian leaders could not concert their response face to face. Now word that the departure will be late means the hour must be chosen again. In Belgrade, Prime Minister Pašić is away from the capital campaigning for the August elections, so the finance minister, Lazar Paču, will receive the ultimatum as acting prime minister.

voices.text: Berlin has waited more than two weeks. The note must go as soon as possible, before Europe’s sympathy over Sarajevo cools.
If the ultimatum arrives while Poincaré is in St Petersburg, France and Russia will join hands on the spot. It must go while the president is at sea.

choices.text: Drop the timing calculations, as Tschirschky urges, and deliver it by day on 23 July even if Poincaré is still in Russia
choices.why: Further delay costs Berlin’s trust and Europe’s sympathy alike
choices.after: News of the ultimatum arrived while Poincaré was still in St Petersburg. The French and Russian leaders discussed a joint response on the spot, and Russia’s position hardened all the sooner.

choices.text: Take Ambassador Mérey’s advice from Rome: inform Italy a day ahead, honoring the consultation duty in Article 7
choices.why: Honor the treaty and Italy will stay in the alliance
choices.after: The Italian foreign minister, San Giuliano, said any change in the Balkan status quo must bring compensation, and raised the question of the Trentino. Just as Vienna had feared, the outline of the ultimatum leaked by way of Rome to St Petersburg.

choices.text: Time it to Poincaré’s departure from Kronstadt: put delivery back one hour, to 6 p.m. on 23 July
choices.why: Keep France and Russia from concerting their answer face to face
choices.after: Around noon on 23 July Giesl received the sealed envelope, and at 6 p.m., at the Serbian Foreign Ministry, he handed the ultimatum to the acting prime minister, Paču. The deadline was 6 p.m. on 25 July. The next day the British foreign secretary, Grey, told the Austrian ambassador that he “had never before seen one State address to another independent State a document of so formidable a character.”

note.text: Article 7 of the Triple Alliance treaty provided that if Austria-Hungary or Italy changed the status quo in the Balkans, they would consult each other beforehand and grant compensation. Fearing leaks to Russia, Vienna did not tell Italy about the ultimatum in advance, and Italy declared its neutrality at the beginning of August.

map.caption: The ultimatum was delivered in Belgrade at 6 p.m. on 23 July; that night Poincaré sailed from Kronstadt.

AT-06.place: Bad Ischl, the Emperor’s summer villa
AT-06.title: A Reply Minutes Before the Deadline

telegram.from: Zemun (telephone report from the border station)
telegram.text: Minister Giesl / Serbian reply a conditional acceptance, point 6 rejected / rupture of relations notified / left Belgrade on the 6:30 p.m. train, crossed the Sava

AT-06.event: At 3 p.m., about three hours before handing over its reply, Serbia had already ordered mobilization, and the government began preparing to move south to Niš.
AT-06.scene: You have come to Bad Ischl to wait out the deadline at the Emperor’s side. Giesl later opened his memoirs with the sentence “July 25, 1914 was a terribly hot day.” The reply Pašić brought to the legation in person, still bearing last-minute handwritten corrections, showed how much work had gone into it. Serbia accepted most of the demands but qualified several, and rejected point 6, on Austrian officials taking part in the investigation, as a violation of its constitution and its code of criminal procedure. Giesl had orders to leave unless the acceptance was unconditional, and his bags were already packed.

voices.who: Your instructions to Minister Giesl (after the Joint Council of 7 July, as Giesl recalled them)
voices.text: However the Serbs react, you must break off relations and leave the country: war is surely coming.

voices.who: Kudashev (Russian chargé d’affaires in Vienna, telegram to Bad Ischl)
voices.text: The Russian government requests an extension of the deadline. It needs time to examine the evidence that Austria has circulated to the powers.

choices.text: Treat the reply as a refusal: break off relations and ask the Emperor tonight to mobilize eight corps against Serbia
choices.why: A conditional acceptance is as good as a refusal
choices.after: That night the Emperor approved partial mobilization, with 28 July set as its first day. Tisza telephoned Giesl at Zemun station across the border and asked, “Did this have to happen?” Giesl said it did. In the streets of Vienna, Budapest and Berlin, crowds sang the Emperor’s Hymn late into the night.

choices.text: Grant the two extra days Russia asked for through Kudashev. Hold off mobilizing in the meantime and watch Russia.
choices.why: Letting Russia save face may keep it from intervening
choices.after: Two days later Serbia’s answer had not changed. In the meantime the Serbian army, already mobilizing, massed troops on the frontier, and mediation proposals arrived from London and St Petersburg.

choices.text: Take the reply, which accepts most demands, as a basis for talks, and settle points 5 and 6 in negotiations with Belgrade
choices.why: That Serbia gave this much ground is itself a gain for the empire
choices.after: Giesl’s train had already left, but Vienna, while announcing the break in relations, added that the door to negotiation remained open. Conrad brandished his resignation, saying the army was being marched up and down for nothing once again, as in 1912.

note.text: In 1914 the soldiers of the common army spoke more than ten languages. The language of command was German; the rank and file learned some eighty German words of command, while officers were expected to learn the languages of the men in their regiments.

AT-07.title: Two Mediation Proposals
AT-07.event: On 26 July the British foreign secretary, Grey, proposed a conference in London of the ambassadors of four powers: Britain, Germany, France and Italy. The same day the Russian foreign minister, Sazonov, proposed to Szápáry, the Austrian ambassador in St Petersburg, that the two countries negotiate directly over the text of the ultimatum. Field Marshal Putnik, the Serbian chief of staff, who had been detained in Budapest on his way home on the night of 25 July, was released the next day on the Emperor’s orders and set off for home by way of Romania.
AT-07.scene: Relations with Serbia are broken, and preparations for partial mobilization against Serbia are under way. Since 26 July Russia has been in its “Period Preparatory to War,” hurrying preparations in the frontier districts. If an ambassadors' conference meets, the Serbian question leaves Vienna’s hands and becomes something for the great powers to bargain over; accept direct talks, and you all but recognize Russia as Serbia’s protector. Yet refuse both, and Britain will conclude that Vienna and Berlin wanted war from the start.

voices.text: The German government says it is passing on the British proposal only as a formality and does not agree with its substance. It asks that Vienna not misunderstand the gesture.
Sazonov is emotional, but he is looking for a way out. Direct talks may be the last way to let Russia save face.

choices.text: Accept Grey’s conference of four ambassadors. Send Mensdorff, but put the empire’s security first on the agenda.
choices.why: To keep Britain neutral, you have to take a seat at the table
choices.after: Preparations began in London for the four ambassadors to meet. Vienna’s hard-line papers wrote that the empire had handed the matter of the Sarajevo murders over to the European powers.

choices.text: Reject both proposals. A dispute between Austria and Serbia cannot be handed to a conference of the great powers.
choices.why: A great-power conference would only strip the empire of its say
choices.after: Vienna did not take up the conference, and on 28 July instructed Szápáry that the text of the ultimatum was not open to discussion. At the Foreign Office in London, the suspicion hardened that Vienna and Berlin had wanted war from the start.

choices.text: Talk directly with Russia, as Sazonov proposes. Discuss how the ultimatum is to be read, but insist that Serbia be punished.
choices.why: Letting Russia save face could keep the war confined to Serbia
choices.after: Szápáry reported that Sazonov had breathed a sigh of relief on receiving the telegram. In Berlin, Jagow was irritated that Vienna was doing a separate deal with Russia.

note.text: The London ambassadors' conference of 1912–1913 set up Albania as an independent state, as Austria demanded, blocking Serbia’s path to the Adriatic. But Vienna also learned that conferences were slow and uncertain, and in October 1913 it forced Serbian troops out of Albania with a unilateral ultimatum.

AT-08.place: Bad Ischl, the Emperor’s summer villa
AT-08.title: Shots at Temes-Kubin

telegram.text: IV Corps command reports / Serbian troops on Danube steamers near Temes-Kubin fired on our forces / fire returned, sizable engagement / casualties unknown

AT-08.scene: You present the eighty-three-year-old Emperor with a submission for a declaration of war. In the covering note you wrote that Serbia’s reply, though worthless in substance, was conciliatory in form, and that unless a clear situation was created, the Triple Entente might attempt a peaceful settlement once again. You have also attached the report that Serbian troops fired first at Temes-Kubin. If Serbia fired first, this becomes a defensive war, which Italy, a member of the Triple Alliance, and the allied Romania would find hard to ignore; but no one has yet confirmed the report.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: By the book, war is declared when operations can begin. Until the sixteenth day of mobilization the army cannot cross the frontier. It would be better to wait until around 12 August.
Mediation proposals are pouring in. Unless we create a fait accompli, London and St Petersburg will take this matter out of Vienna’s hands.

choices.text: Declare war, but leave out the unconfirmed Temes-Kubin report and put only the facts before the Emperor
choices.why: A pretext won by deceiving the Emperor will not last
choices.after: The Emperor thought it over for another day before signing. With the claim that Serbia had fired first gone, Social Democratic papers and the governments in Rome and Bucharest began to ask whether this was really a defensive war.

choices.text: Delay the declaration to suit Conrad’s timetable, timing it for about 12 August, when the army can cross the frontier
choices.why: A declaration with no operations behind it only gives the enemy time
choices.after: The declaration of war was not sent, and Vienna began to discuss the London and St Petersburg mediation proposals again.

choices.text: Declare war at once and create a fait accompli. Put the Temes-Kubin report into the submission and the declaration.
choices.why: Only a fait accompli can head off mediation
choices.after: The Emperor signed on 27 July, but no engagement of the kind reported had taken place at Temes-Kubin. You struck out the unconfirmed passage and sent the declaration of war by telegram on the morning of 28 July; with relations broken, it reached the Serbian government at Niš by way of Romania. Only the next day did you tell the Emperor that the passage had been deleted and ask for his approval after the fact.

note.text: Army records show only that near Temes-Kubin (today Kovin in Serbia) a Serbian steamer came under Austro-Hungarian fire, stopped, and was released after inspection. The historian Rauchensteiner doubts whether the telegram reporting an engagement ever actually existed.

pressure.title: Slipping Out of Vienna’s Hands
pressure.text: In your submission you wrote that unless a clear situation was created, the Triple Entente might attempt a peaceful settlement once again. One reading holds that you were hurried by the memory of how slow and uncertain the London ambassadors' conference of 1912–1913 had proved for Vienna. As mediation proposals pile up, each day the declaration of war is put off may be a day in which the Serbian question slips out of Vienna’s hands.

AT-09.title: Halt in Belgrade

telegram.text: Bethmann Hollweg to Tschirschky / refusing even an exchange of views with St Petersburg would be a grave error / Germany will fulfill its alliance obligations / but refuses to be dragged by Vienna into a world conflagration with its advice ignored / put this to Berchtold at once and in earnest

AT-09.event: Before dawn on 29 July, monitors of the Danube Flotilla and the batteries at Zemun shelled Belgrade. The same day Russia announced the partial mobilization of four military districts: Odessa, Kiev, Moscow and Kazan.
AT-09.scene: On the morning of 28 July Kaiser Wilhelm read Serbia’s reply and wrote that with it every reason for war dropped away. His proposal: the Austrian army should occupy Belgrade alone as a pledge, stop there, and negotiate while it sees whether Serbia keeps its promises. Today Ambassador Tschirschky has come to you with Bethmann Hollweg’s telegrams. Another, which arrived in the same early hours, advises accepting British mediation on the basis of an occupation of Belgrade or other places. Berlin, which wrote the blank check three weeks ago, is now trying to restrain Vienna.

voices.who: Bethmann Hollweg (German chancellor, telegram of 30 July)
voices.text: We are, of course, ready to fulfil the obligations of our alliance, but must decline to be drawn wantonly into a world conflagration by Vienna, without having any regard paid to our counsel.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Belgrade is only a frontier town. The main Serbian army is in the south; stop at a pledge, and the army throws away a war half won.

choices.text: Attach conditions that amount to refusal: continue against Serbia, and accept mediation only if Russia stops mobilizing
choices.why: Stopping at Belgrade would be another half victory
choices.after: Vienna put off its answer another day; then, at the Joint Council of 31 July, it agreed to accept British mediation only if operations against Serbia continued and Russia stopped mobilizing, which amounted to a refusal. Szápáry was instructed to resume talks with Sazonov, but very little time was left.

choices.text: Accept the Wilhelm–Grey plan: occupy Belgrade as a pledge, halt there, and announce you will accept great-power mediation
choices.why: This is the last chance to keep both Germany and Britain on side
choices.after: That night Tschirschky wired Berlin that Vienna had at last accepted the “Halt in Belgrade.” Conrad went back to the General Staff and locked his door.

note.text: Belgrade lay where the Sava meets the Danube, just across the Austro-Hungarian frontier. Zemun (Semlin in German), across the river, belonged to Croatia-Slavonia under the Hungarian crown, so the Serbian capital was within artillery range from the first day of the war.

map.caption: Belgrade, where the Sava meets the Danube, lay within range of the batteries at Zemun across the river.

AT-10.title: Who Rules in Berlin?

telegram.at: Sent 30 July, received 7:45 a.m. on 31 July
telegram.text: Moltke to Conrad / stand firm against Russian mobilization / Austria-Hungary must be preserved / mobilize against Russia at once / Germany will mobilize / compel Italy to her alliance duty with compensations

AT-10.event: On the afternoon of 30 July Nicholas II, won over by Sazonov and the General Staff, approved general mobilization once more; the whole Russian army is now on the move.
AT-10.scene: On your desk lie two telegrams from Berlin. One is Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg’s warning that Germany will not be dragged into a world conflagration; the other is Moltke’s call, as Chief of the General Staff, to mobilize against Russia at once. Conrad’s memoirs record how you reacted on hearing Moltke’s telegram. Russian general mobilization now means that troops beyond the Galician frontier are on the move as well.

voices.who: Moltke (Chief of the German General Staff, telegram to Conrad)
voices.text: Stand firm against Russian mobilization. Austria-Hungary must be preserved; mobilize against Russia at once. Germany will mobilize. Compel Italy to fulfill her duty as an ally by means of compensations.

voices.who: Berchtold (you, as recorded in Conrad’s memoirs)
voices.text: That beats everything! Who is in charge: Moltke or Bethmann?

choices.text: Heed Bethmann Hollweg’s warning. Halt operations against Serbia and accept British mediation together with Berlin.
choices.why: Ignore the German chancellor’s warning and you lose the alliance too
choices.after: Bethmann Hollweg was relieved, but Moltke said it was already too late. Whether Russia would stop mobilizing now depended on the Tsar’s resolve in St Petersburg.

choices.text: As Moltke urges, ask the Emperor for general mobilization against Russia too, and keep the Serbian operation going
choices.why: With Russia on the move, you must stand with Germany
choices.after: At midday on 31 July Franz Joseph signed the order for general mobilization, with 4 August set as its first day. The next day Germany declared war on Russia.

choices.text: Concentrate on the Serbian front. Hold Galicia with defensive forces only and leave the war with Russia to Germany.
choices.why: Avoid facing Russia, and the war could stay in the Balkans
choices.after: Moltke was furious that his ally had broken its word. Russian mobilization did not stop; Germany went to war with Russia and France after all, and Vienna could not stay out of that war.

note.text: The General Staff’s war plans were divided into Plan B, against Serbia alone, and Plan R, against Russia as well. The Second Army, the so-called “B-Staffel,” could be sent either way, and where it went decided the balance of forces in Galicia.

pressure.title: Two Berlins
pressure.text: Tisza, Stürgkh and Burián were present when Moltke’s telegram was read to you. In the Germany that wrote the blank check three weeks ago, the chancellor now says stop and the Chief of the General Staff says hurry. Whichever voice you follow, Austria-Hungary cannot face Russia without Germany, and the fear of being abandoned if you do not move has gripped the whole Foreign Ministry since early July.

AT-11.place: Vienna, Railway Bureau of the General Staff
AT-11.title: The Second Army’s Trains
AT-11.event: On 31 July Germany proclaimed a “state of imminent danger of war” and sent Russia an ultimatum with a 12-hour deadline. Russian troops are massing beyond the Galician frontier.
AT-11.scene: In step with mobilization against Serbia, the Second Army’s trains have already left for the south. Conrad now wants to turn the Second Army north to Galicia, but the head of the Railway Bureau, Colonel Straub, says that changing the timetables all at once will bring the whole network to a standstill. On 30 July alone 31 trains left for the south, and 42 the next day; more than a million men have to be moved. Since around 1907 Conrad has secretly loved Gina von Reininghaus, the wife of an industrialist, and written her thousands of letters, many never sent; some historians believe that his hope of marrying her if he became a war hero colored his judgment.

voices.who: Straub (head of the General Staff’s Railway Bureau)
voices.text: If we turn back trains that have already left, both the southern and the northern lines will seize up. The Second Army must go to the Serbian frontier and detrain, then be loaded again and sent to Galicia as soon as the lines are clear.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Every day we are late in Galicia means taking the full force of the first Russian blow. But leave Serbia alone and the reason for starting this war disappears.

choices.text: Turn the Second Army’s trains north at once, as Conrad first wanted, trusting the rail chaos to clear in a few days
choices.why: The first battle in Galicia will decide the whole war
choices.after: Hundreds of trains stood stalled at stations. The Second Army may have reached Galicia a few days sooner, but General Potiorek, who led the offensive against Serbia in the south, was left with far fewer troops.

choices.text: Keep the Second Army in the south, as Potiorek wants. Finish Serbia first and trust the German army in Galicia.
choices.why: First achieve what this war was started for
choices.after: Moltke protested that Austria had broken its promise to hold the east. In Galicia the Austro-Hungarian forces were heavily outnumbered by the Russians, while the Serbian army fell back into the mountains and held on.

choices.text: Follow Colonel Straub: let the Second Army detrain in the south and move to Galicia as soon as the lines clear
choices.why: If the timetables collapse, both fronts are lost
choices.after: Part of the Second Army fought briefly on the Sava front and was moved to Galicia only after mid-August, arriving too late for the decisive moment and with reduced strength. Churchill later wrote in The Unknown War (1931): “It left Potiorek before it could win him a victory; it returned to Conrad in time to participate in his defeat.”

note.text: In August 1914 Austria-Hungary lent the German army its Škoda 30.5 cm siege mortars, together with their crews, and they were used to smash the Belgian forts at Liège, Namur and Antwerp.

map.caption: On the Galician front, where the Second Army arrived late, Lemberg fell to the Russians in early September 1914.

AT-12.title: The Answers from Rome and Bucharest

telegram.text: Italian government decides on neutrality / holds that the Triple Alliance is defensive and that Vienna acted without prior consultation / wishes to continue discussing compensation

AT-12.event: Today in Romania, King Carol I called a crown council, revealed the secret treaty he had made with the Triple Alliance side and argued for entering the war, but most of those present, including Prime Minister Brătianu, chose neutrality.
AT-12.scene: The Joint Council of 31 July decided to reject Italy’s demand for compensation, while allowing that compensation could be discussed if Serbian territory were occupied for a long time, and only if Italy fulfilled its alliance obligations. In the week before, the German government had pressed Vienna almost daily to come around to Italy’s view, and Wilhelm II even tried to work on the war minister Krobatin in person. You thought 10 million crowns well spent if it swayed the Italian press, but Rome chose neutrality all the same. Germany has begun to talk of territorial concessions to Romania too, and there will soon be talk of giving up Radautz and Suczawa in Bukovina.

voices.who: István Tisza (Hungarian prime minister, on proposals to cede territory; date unknown)
voices.text: A state that hands over territories from its own body, in order to deter a neighbour that is inclined towards treachery from committing complete betrayal, degrades itself in the eyes of the whole world.
The German government believes this is no time to argue over how to interpret the treaty. Meet the wishes of Italy and Romania as far as you possibly can.

choices.text: Refuse to cede territory. Hold to the Council decision of 31 July: compensation only if Italy enters the war.
choices.why: A state that gives away its own land cannot keep its standing
choices.after: Italy stayed neutral; Vienna took the question up again at the Joint Council of 8 August, but even then no cession of the Trentino was offered. Italy entered the war on the Entente side in May 1915.

choices.text: As Berlin urges, ask the Emperor to cede part of the Trentino as the price of bringing Italy from neutrality into the war
choices.why: Giving up land costs less than facing another front
choices.after: Franz Joseph replied that he would rather abdicate than give up the Trentino. The Emperor did in fact say as much, and Vienna’s offers never went as far as Italy wanted.

choices.text: Follow Germany’s advice and offer southern Bukovina to Romania, strengthening King Carol’s case for war
choices.why: Bring Romania in before it strikes from behind
choices.after: Tisza objected that giving land to Romania would spill over into the question of Transylvania, and the Emperor refused as well. Romania entered the war on the Entente side in August 1916.

note.text: King Carol I of Romania came from the German house of Hohenzollern and in 1883 concluded a secret treaty with the Triple Alliance side. But some argue that the Tisza government’s treatment of the Romanians in the Kingdom of Hungary made it hard for Bucharest to side with Vienna, and Archduke Franz Ferdinand had disagreed with Tisza on this very question.

map.caption: In early August 1914 both Italy, a Triple Alliance partner, and Romania, a secret ally, chose neutrality.

pressure.title: The Emperor’s Land
pressure.text: Franz Joseph has said he would rather abdicate than give up the Trentino. Tisza, too, firmly opposes ceding territory to Italy and Romania, and at the Joint Council of 8 August the Austrian and Hungarian prime ministers spoke with one voice on the Trentino. Berlin, by contrast, presses almost daily for concessions.

AT-13.title: The Declaration of War on Russia
AT-13.event: On 5 August Montenegro declared war on Austria-Hungary. Germany had declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, and Britain went to war with Germany on 4 August.
AT-13.scene: Four days have passed since Germany went to war with Russia, but Austria-Hungary has not yet declared war on Russia. On 1 August the Emperor decided to take the offensive both against Serbia in the south and against Russia in the north, and Conrad wants to declare war only after mobilization and deployment have gone as far as possible. Almost every day Vienna assures London and Paris that the empire has no hostile intentions toward the Entente and wants only reparation from Serbia. When to send the declaration to St Petersburg is now a question of diplomacy and railway timetables at once.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: The declaration should come when deployment is nearly complete. Send it after the trains to Galicia have run at least one more day.
Grey hints that he does not want to fight Austria. But if France demands it, Britain will not hold out for long.

choices.text: Declare war on Russia on 6 August, on Conrad’s timetable, and assure London and Paris that you mean them no hostility
choices.why: Buy time to finish deploying while avoiding war with Britain
choices.after: On 6 August Ambassador Szápáry handed over the declaration of war in St Petersburg and left Russia. The same day Conrad promised the German army two batteries of 30.5 cm mortars for the western front. France broke off relations on 10 August, claiming that an Austrian corps had reached the French frontier, and on 12 August Britain too declared war on Austria-Hungary.

choices.text: Declare nothing unless Russia crosses the Galician frontier first. Keep the war confined to Serbia.
choices.why: Never declaring war first might spare you a war with the Entente
choices.after: Moltke protested that his ally was breaking its word. Russian troops massed on the Galician frontier regardless, and a few days later Vienna sent its declaration after all. All the while, Britain and France regarded Austria-Hungary as Germany’s partner.

choices.text: As Berlin urges through Tschirschky, declare war today, to show you have entered the same war as Germany
choices.why: Arousing your ally’s suspicion is worse than delaying deployment
choices.after: The declaration reached St Petersburg a day early. Berlin welcomed it, but Conrad complained that his army would meet the first clashes on the Galician frontier before its deployment was complete.

note.text: By early August 1914 Vienna had itself declared war on two countries, Serbia (28 July) and Russia (6 August). Montenegro declared war first, on 5 August, and France and Britain were at war with Austria-Hungary by around 12 August.

AT-01X.title: Tschirschky’s Warning
AT-01X.event: On 1 July Tisza, the Hungarian prime minister, sent the Emperor a memorandum warning that to use Sarajevo as a pretext for punishment, with no evidence that the Serbian government was involved, would be a fatal mistake.
AT-01X.scene: Hearing that you have decided to ask for immediate mobilization, the German ambassador in Vienna, Tschirschky, comes to the Foreign Ministry. He says he has not yet received instructions from Berlin, but that starting a war with no assurance that Italy and Romania will not side with Serbia would be very dangerous. Vienna knows next to nothing of how Berlin sees the affair, and it is not yet settled whether the German Kaiser will come to the funeral. Before you see the Emperor, you must decide whether to move the army without knowing your ally’s mind.

voices.text: I have no instructions from Berlin yet. But let me say plainly that drawing the sword without knowing where Italy and Romania stand would be very dangerous.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Spend two weeks asking Germany’s opinion and Europe’s sympathy will cool, and with it our case for striking Serbia. Germany will follow in the end.

choices.text: Heed Tschirschky’s warning. Send Hoyos to Berlin with the Emperor’s letter to learn Germany’s intentions first.
choices.why: You cannot move the army without knowing your ally’s mind
choices.after: Conrad’s draft submission went into a drawer. On the night of 4 July your chef de cabinet, Hoyos, boarded the night train to Berlin with Franz Joseph’s personal letter and the Matscheko memorandum, revised after Sarajevo.
choices.realNote: Hoyos’s mission happened as described, but there was no earlier push for immediate mobilization.

choices.text: Press on as Conrad says: ask the Emperor to approve mobilization, and merely inform Germany of the decision
choices.why: Germany will have no choice but to follow
choices.after: Tschirschky went back to his embassy stony-faced and reported to Berlin that Vienna meant to act without consulting its ally. You are to see the Emperor at Schönbrunn on 3 July.

note.text: On 28 June 1881 Serbia under the Obrenović dynasty signed a secret convention with Austria-Hungary, undertaking not to conclude political treaties with other states without first consulting Vienna. This relationship, which made Serbia in effect a protectorate, collapsed after the coup of 1903.

AT-02X.title: The Emperor’s Question
AT-02X.scene: Having hurried back from Bad Ischl on 29 June, the Emperor sits at the plain desk in his study at Schönbrunn. Eighty-three years old, he came to the throne in 1848 at eighteen; in the 66 years since, he has lost his brother, his only son and the Empress one after another, and now his heir, Franz Ferdinand, too. When you put Conrad’s plan for immediate mobilization before him, the Emperor asks first about Germany. By Conrad’s reckoning, partial mobilization against Serbia will take a little over two weeks, and soldiers of several corps are at home on harvest leave.

voices.text: Are you certain Germany will stand with us? Without that certainty we cannot face Russia. And what does Tisza say?

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Your Majesty, every day of delay cools Europe’s sympathy while Serbia gathers troops on the frontier. If not now, the chance will never come again.

choices.text: Ask for approval to mobilize, as Conrad says, counting on the Emperor’s authority to override Tisza’s opposition
choices.why: Each day’s delay costs a chance that will not return
choices.after: The Emperor was silent for a long while, then allowed preparations for mobilization. That evening Tisza sent a telegram saying that the Hungarian government could not take responsibility for the decision.

choices.text: Admit you cannot answer the Emperor’s question with confidence. Send Hoyos to Berlin to learn Germany’s intentions first.
choices.why: Without a German pledge, even the Emperor will not move
choices.realNote: Hoyos’s mission happened as described, but no plan for immediate mobilization was ever put to the Emperor beforehand.
choices.after: The Emperor nodded, and you went back to sounding out your ally first. On the night of 4 July Hoyos boarded the night train to Berlin with the Emperor’s personal letter and the Matscheko memorandum.

note.text: Franz Joseph made a habit of never summoning the Austrian and Hungarian prime ministers together. Even on the gravest matters of the Dual Monarchy, he saw the two men separately.

AT-02T.place: Bad Ischl, the Emperor’s summer villa (Kaiservilla)
AT-02T.title: Will the Emperor Defy Hungary?
AT-02T.scene: At the Kaiservilla, ringed by the mountains and rivers of the Salzkammergut, the old Emperor receives you in uniform. He came to the throne in 1848 at eighteen and is now in his 66th year as Emperor. In that time his brother Maximilian was shot in Mexico, his only son Rudolf took his own life at Mayerling, and the Empress Elisabeth was assassinated in Geneva. Now he has lost his nephew and heir, Franz Ferdinand, too. You ask to bypass Tisza, but the Emperor has not forgotten his head-on clash with the Hungarian parliament in 1905–1906.

voices.text: Dismiss the Hungarian prime minister and the parliament in Budapest will rise up. To make war, both halves of the monarchy must stand together.
Your Majesty, we need only bring Count Tisza around. The longer we wait, the more Berlin will see Vienna as a hopeless ally.

choices.text: Bow to the Emperor’s wishes. Return to Vienna, sit down with Tisza and hear out his condition: no annexation.
choices.why: Defy Hungary and the war cannot even be fought
choices.after: The Emperor gave a short nod, as if relieved. You went back to Vienna to prepare for your meeting with Tisza.

choices.text: Press the Emperor again: obtain his approval without Tisza and begin preparing mobilization against Serbia at once
choices.why: Waiting for Hungary’s consent will cost you the chance
choices.after: The Emperor was silent for a long while, then allowed preparations for mobilization. That evening Tisza sent a telegram saying he could not take responsibility for the decision.

note.text: When the Hungarian parliament defied Vienna in 1905–1906, demanding Hungarian as a language of command in the common army, the Emperor sent troops in February 1906 to dissolve it. The memory still weighed on relations between the two halves of the monarchy in 1914.

AT-03X.title: Cancel the Harvest Leave
AT-03X.scene: To mobilize, the soldiers on harvest leave must first be recalled. But call the men out of the July wheat fields and the harvest is ruined, and every intelligence officer across the border will notice. The German ambassador in Vienna, Tschirschky, reports that Berlin wants swift action but is annoyed that there was no consultation beforehand. Remembering how the troop buildup of winter 1912 came to nothing, the officer corps says that this time it must go all the way.

voices.text: Recall the men on leave and you ruin the harvest, and all Europe will notice. By 25 July they will be back of their own accord.
Berlin supports swift action. But it hopes never again to learn from the newspapers what its ally intends to do.

choices.text: Cancel harvest leave and announce partial mobilization of eight corps against Serbia. Time matters more than the harvest.
choices.why: Better to lose the harvest than to lose time
choices.after: Returning soldiers crowded every station, and Vienna’s newspapers wrote that the hour of retribution had come. That night the military attachés in St Petersburg and Belgrade sent telegrams saying the same thing.

choices.text: Hold off any announcement, as Krobatin says, and prepare quietly until the men return from leave on 25 July
choices.why: Reveal your preparations and the advantage of surprise is gone
choices.after: The mobilization orders were filed away unannounced. In the end Vienna went back to the slow road: an envoy to Berlin to confirm its support, and the work of persuading Tisza.

note.text: In July 1914 Conrad said that the futile mobilization of 1912 had left the army so exhausted that mobilization could now be ordered only if war was certain.

AT-04X.title: Tisza’s Resignation
AT-04X.scene: Tisza, up from Budapest, sits before you with his resignation in his hand. He knows better than anyone that Magyars make up only slightly more than half the population of the Kingdom of Hungary. Annex Serbia and bring in more South Slavs, and Hungary might become a minority within the empire. Across the border Serbia, too, is hurrying to mobilize, and from St Petersburg comes a warning that Russia will not stand by while Serbia’s independence is threatened.

voices.text: Without a declaration that no Serbian territory will be annexed, Hungary cannot agree to this war, least of all to a war that would bring more Slavs into the empire.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: The army is already on the move. Even a 48-hour deadline is too long. Twenty-four hours is enough.

choices.text: Accept Tisza’s condition and announce that no Serbian territory will be annexed. Keep Hungary on board and press ahead.
choices.why: The war cannot be fought without Hungary
choices.after: Tisza withdrew his resignation. The declaration of no annexation softened London and Rome a little, but in Berlin Wilhelm grumbled that it was a feeble statement.

choices.text: Go ahead unconditionally, as Conrad says: send a 24-hour ultimatum and cross the frontier at once
choices.why: A quick victory will quiet Hungary’s discontent as well
choices.after: Tisza’s resignation lay on the Emperor’s desk, neither refused nor accepted. Serbia did not answer the ultimatum, and gunfire began along the banks of the Sava.

note.text: In the 1910 census, people whose mother tongue was Magyar made up slightly more than half the population of the Kingdom of Hungary, excluding Croatia-Slavonia. That is why Tisza feared any increase in the number of Slavs.

AT-04Xa.title: Rome’s Bill

telegram.text: Embassy in Rome / Foreign Minister San Giuliano: action against Serbia without prior consultation violates the Triple Alliance / compensation under Article 7 demanded even for temporary occupation

AT-04Xa.scene: With the Austrian army hurrying its mobilization, Italy has presented its bill. Citing Article 7 of the Triple Alliance treaty, Italy argues that if Austria-Hungary takes any territory in the Balkans, even temporarily, it must pay compensation. What Italy wants is the Austrian Trentino, and Berlin, too, advises concessions to keep Italy in line. But the old Emperor will not hear of giving away the empire’s land.

voices.text: Berlin does not want to lose Italy. Give up even part of the Trentino and Italy will at least keep up a friendly neutrality.
Start giving land to Italy and Romania will demand the same. Hungary cannot open that road.

choices.text: Reject San Giuliano’s demand. Reply that a punitive war without annexation gives no grounds for Article 7 compensation.
choices.why: Give in to a compensation claim once and there is no end to it
choices.after: San Giuliano again stressed that the Triple Alliance was a defensive alliance, and the Rome papers wrote that Vienna was ignoring its ally. Hardly anyone in Vienna still expects Italy to join this war.

choices.text: Keep the Trentino, but recognize Italy’s share in the Albanian question to buy Rome’s friendly neutrality
choices.why: Pay the price somewhere other than the empire’s own land
choices.after: Rome took the offer under consideration but put off a firm answer. Still, the Italian government did not publicly condemn Vienna’s action, and Berlin was somewhat relieved.

note.text: In 1914 Vienna informed Italy of the ultimatum only on 23 July, and its text reached Rome a day later. When Germany urged ceding the Trentino, Franz Joseph said he would rather abdicate than give it up.

AT-05X.title: Facing Belgrade
AT-05X.scene: Just across the Sava stands Kalemegdan, Belgrade’s fortress. The Serbian government has already moved south to Niš, and the main Serbian army has withdrawn inland to wait for the Austrians. The monitors of the Danube Flotilla are ready to open fire. Intelligence is coming in that Russia is preparing a partial mobilization, while Berlin signals that a pledge occupation will be enough.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Belgrade is only the beginning. This war ends only when we catch the main Serbian army in the interior.
Berlin believes that holding the capital as a pledge is enough. Do not give Russia a pretext to intervene.

choices.text: Take Berlin’s hint: occupy Belgrade and stop there. Hold the capital as a pledge and open negotiations.
choices.why: Hold the capital and you win without provoking Russia
choices.after: The Austrian army entered Belgrade without much resistance. Conrad’s aide reported that his hand had shaken as he signed the order to halt the advance.

choices.text: Do as Conrad says: push past Belgrade into the interior, find the main Serbian army and destroy it
choices.why: Fail to break their main army and you fight the same war again
choices.after: The army passed Belgrade and moved into the hills to the south. As at Cer in August 1914, the Serbian army was waiting for the invaders, using the ground to its advantage.

note.text: In 1914, at around 2 a.m. on 29 July, the Danube Flotilla monitors Temes, Bodrog and Számos opened the first bombardment of Belgrade (some accounts name the Bodrog as the ship that fired the first shell). Monitors were low armored vessels built to bombard from shallow rivers.

AT-05XA.title: An Occupied Capital
AT-05XA.scene: The Austrian flag has been raised over the Kalemegdan fortress. The Serbian government and the main army have pulled back south, while the mayor, the police and the shopkeepers remain in the city. How the occupation is run will shape both the terms of negotiation and the reaction of the empire’s own Serbs. The Croat-Serb Coalition, the majority in the Croatian-Slavonian diet, has worked with the Tisza government since reaching a compromise with it at the end of 1913, but after the anti-Serb riots in Sarajevo and Zagreb in late June its Serb deputies have grown uneasy.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Occupied territory must be ruled by martial law. Dissolve the anti-Austrian societies, find the people involved and bring them before military courts.
Every piece of news from Belgrade goes straight to the diet in Zagreb. If the occupation turns harsh, the Coalition can no longer work with Budapest.

choices.text: Impose military rule as Conrad demands: dissolve groups like Narodna Odbrana and try those involved by court-martial
choices.why: Look weak in occupied land and resistance grows
choices.after: Belgrade’s newspaper offices and the societies' headquarters were closed. Russian papers called it persecution of Slav brothers, and in Zagreb the Serb deputies put off attending the diet.

choices.text: Heed Skerlecz: leave the city administration alone, use troops only for order, and demand cooperation and reparation
choices.why: A harsh occupation would turn the empire’s Serbs against it
choices.after: The mayor of Belgrade sat down with the commander of the occupying force. Conrad was unhappy with what he called a half-occupation, but reactions in London and Rome were noticeably milder.

note.text: The Croat-Serb Coalition, a party alliance formed in 1905 by Croat and Serb politicians, won majorities in the Croatian-Slavonian diet elections of 1908 and 1913. The Croatian constitution was suspended in the spring of 1912; in 1913 Tisza sent his confidant Skerlecz as Ban and reached a compromise with the Coalition.

AT-05XB.place: Northern Serbia, the hills of the Šumadija
AT-05XB.title: Into the Mountains
AT-05XB.scene: Past Belgrade, the Austrian army has entered the hills and forests of the Šumadija to the south. The Serbian army avoids a head-on fight, falling back and cutting bridges and railways as it goes, and the government has already moved to Niš. The farther south the army goes, the longer its supply lines, and from the Galician frontier in the north come more and more reports of Russian movements. Taking the arsenal at Kragujevac would cut off the Serbian army’s supply of weapons, but it would also take the army that much farther from the Russian frontier.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Take the arsenal and the Serbian army loses the weapons to fight with. Stop here and we will have to fight the same war again in a few years.

voices.who: Potiorek (governor of Bosnia, commander in the Balkans)
voices.text: Serbian reservists are hiding in every valley. Go farther before the railways are repaired and the army will wear itself out first.

choices.text: Push on south to the Kragujevac arsenal, as Conrad wants, and cut off the Serbian army’s supply of weapons
choices.why: Cut off their source of arms and the war ends
choices.after: The army moved south, repairing broken bridges as it went. The Serbian army avoided a major battle and withdrew into the mountains, and in St Petersburg voices grew louder that something must be done before Serbia collapsed.

choices.text: Heed Potiorek and halt the advance. Hold northern Serbia and present your terms by way of Belgrade.
choices.why: Keep what you have won before the supply lines stretch too far
choices.after: The army halted on a defensive line south of the Sava and the Danube. Conrad complained that once again only half the army was being used, and the Serbian government at Niš sent word by way of Romania that it was ready to hear terms.

note.text: The General Staff’s Plan B placed the main thrust in the west, from Bosnia, with Belgrade to be occupied only after a large part of Serbia had been taken. In 1914 the Austrian army that crossed the Drina in August was defeated by the Serbs at Cer and retreated.

map.caption: Kragujevac held the Serbian army’s arsenal, and Niš the wartime government. In August 1914 the first major battle was in fact fought to the west, on Mount Cer.

AT-06X.title: Russia’s Choice

telegram.text: Ambassador Szápáry / Russia preparing partial mobilization of four military districts on the Austrian frontier / Sazonov: violation of Serbian independence cannot be tolerated / but mentions room for negotiation

AT-06X.scene: Russia is about to decide whether to back down, as in the Bosnian crisis of 1909, or to go all the way this time. Tsar Nicholas II dreads war, but the newspapers and ministers in St Petersburg say they will never again accept humiliation. Germany has promised to fight alongside Austria if Russia moves, but when that promise turns into action depends on the timetables of the German General Staff. The Tsar’s decision may turn on the signal Vienna sends.

voices.text: Sazonov has hinted that Russia could accept Austria’s punishment of Serbia, provided Serbia’s independence is guaranteed. He needs a written commitment.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: If Russia mobilizes, Galicia is in danger. Russian mobilization must be answered with mobilization.

choices.text: Take Szápáry’s advice and pledge in writing to Russia: no annexation, respect for Serbian sovereignty, a withdrawal schedule
choices.why: Give Russia grounds to step back and the war stays small
choices.after: The Tsar put off partial mobilization. The hard-liners in St Petersburg were furious, but Sazonov could now tell his colleagues that this time diplomacy had won.

choices.text: As Conrad says, answer Russian mobilization with mobilization, and send troops to the Galician frontier as well
choices.why: Show Russia weakness and it will only push further
choices.after: As Russia and Austria traded mobilization orders, the General Staff in Berlin took out the files of its western campaign plan. The punitive war in the Balkans is on the verge of spreading to the borders of Germany and France.

note.text: In June 1914 Russia enacted its large-scale rearmament program, the “Great Programme,” due for completion in 1917. That is why the soldiers in Vienna and Berlin believed that time was not on their side.

AT-07X.title: An Invitation from London
AT-07X.scene: The British foreign secretary, Grey, proposes a conference of great-power ambassadors to settle the Serbian question. The Austrian army has crossed the Sava and stands on Serbian soil, while the Russian army waits near the frontier for mobilization orders. Berlin says that this time, too, it will follow Vienna’s decision, but Moltke’s General Staff says that every day of delay is a loss. Stop here, and the war of 1914 could end as a short Balkan war.

voices.text: Serbia has already been punished. Go further and the Hungarian plain will become a battlefield against Russia.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Go to that conference and the powers will bring Serbia back to life. We cannot stop before the Serbian army is broken.

choices.text: Go to the London conference, as Tisza says. Hold Belgrade only until Serbia carries out its promises.
choices.why: Keep what you have gained and end the war in the Balkans
choices.after: Ambassador Mensdorff entered the conference room in London. But in a Europe where mobilization orders have already been exchanged, whether the conference can do its work depends on the timetables of the general staffs.

choices.text: Refuse the conference, as Conrad says. Fight on until the Serbian army is broken and all of Serbia is occupied.
choices.why: A conference would only let the powers revive Serbia
choices.after: Russia answered with general mobilization, and Germany declared war on Russia and then on France. The punitive war in the Balkans became a European war, following the course events actually took.

note.text: Historians disagree: some argue that if Austria had struck Serbia swiftly right after Sarajevo, Europe would have accepted the fait accompli; others argue that Russia would have intervened anyway.

AT-03M.title: After Hartwig’s Death

telegram.text: Minister Giesl / Russian minister Hartwig collapsed and died while visiting this legation / rumors of poisoning in the city

AT-03M.scene: Since choosing Tisza’s path at the meeting of 7 July, you have been preparing demands that Serbia can accept. But now Hartwig, who spoke for Russia in Belgrade, has collapsed and died at the Austrian legation. The question is no longer only what to demand but through whom to say it. Go through St Petersburg, and Vienna itself acknowledges Russia as Serbia’s guardian; deal with Belgrade alone, and Pašić may play for time, counting on Russian support.

voices.text: Ask Sazonov to calm Serbia and Russia becomes the mediator in this affair. We would be handing him the chance to avenge the humiliation of 1909.
Serbia is not a country that moves only when Russia tells it to. We must speak to Belgrade directly, but as gentlemen.

choices.text: Ask Sazonov to persuade Serbia to cooperate with the investigation, putting Russia on the side of the solution
choices.why: Bring Russia in, and Serbia will follow its lead
choices.after: Sazonov replied courteously but made clear that Russia could not agree to demands that harmed Serbia’s sovereignty. Tschirschky reported to Berlin that Vienna had left the matter to Russia.

choices.text: Deal directly with Belgrade, as Tisza says. Tell Russia only what the note contains, and only after it is sent.
choices.why: Russia cannot be recognized as Serbia’s guardian
choices.after: You decided to keep the note a matter between Vienna and Belgrade. The St Petersburg papers went on printing the story that Hartwig had been poisoned.

note.text: When Serbia advanced toward the Adriatic in 1912, Russia did not help it seize Albanian land, while Hartwig went beyond his instructions in hinting at Russian support for Serbia. Whether Serbia was merely Russia’s proxy is debated; historians such as Clark stress that Belgrade pursued its own goals.

AT-04M.title: A Note Serbia Can Accept
AT-04M.scene: You and Tisza begin drafting a note that Serbia can accept. Forgách and Hoyos protest that this overturns the conclusion of the 7 July meeting, and at the War Ministry Conrad complains that the army is once again being marched up and down for nothing. The note is meant not as a pretext for war but to bring the backers of the Sarajevo plot to light and have the anti-Austrian societies in Serbia dissolved. Berlin’s man in Vienna, Ambassador Tschirschky, is at a loss as to how to report all this.

voices.text: This must be handled as gentlemen. If Serbia refuses, Europe will side with the empire; if it accepts, we have won without bloodshed.
Berlin will read this as weakness. Germany did not write a blank check for the sake of a diplomatic note.

choices.text: Demand an international inquiry with neutral jurists and punishment of the officers involved, with a generous five-day deadline
choices.why: Only with neutral observers can the inquiry be trusted
choices.after: The draft even named Swiss and Dutch jurists. Forgách sat a long time before the signature line without lifting his pen.

choices.text: Demand only a public apology from the Serbian government and the dissolution of Narodna Odbrana, leaving no grounds to refuse
choices.why: The smaller the demands, the harder they are to refuse
choices.after: The note was short and polite. Vienna’s hard-line papers asked whether the Archduke’s life was worth a single letter of apology.

note.text: In July 1914 Tisza did insist that Serbia be dealt with in a gentlemanly way, and Berchtold complained to the German ambassador that such methods were unsuited to an opponent like Serbia.

AT-05M.title: Berlin’s Disappointment

telegram.text: Szögyény / German government surprised at the mild terms of Vienna’s note / Kaiser Wilhelm deeply disappointed / view that if this chance is missed the empire’s future cannot be assured

AT-05M.scene: When the moderate note was delivered in Belgrade, Berlin reacted coldly. Germany had seen the crisis as a chance for Austria to regain strength in the Balkans and, at the same time, to show the alliance’s solidarity before Russia finished rearming. Now Berlin’s diplomats whisper that Vienna is a useless ally. Back in early July a diplomat at the embassy in Berlin had warned that Germany would abandon Vienna if Austria did not act.

voices.who: Haymerle (counselor at the embassy in Berlin, letter of 8 July)
voices.text: Here at the Foreign Office, we are being pressured from all sides into taking action. The mood is overwhelmingly supportive of us if we get going, otherwise, I would almost say, we are likely to be abandoned as a hopeless case.
Germany cannot abandon the empire. Austria-Hungary is the only ally Germany has left. Berlin’s disappointment will pass.

choices.text: Work on Berlin through Szögyény: a diplomatic victory won without bloodshed is a victory for the alliance too
choices.why: In the end Germany cannot abandon its only ally
choices.after: Bethmann Hollweg reluctantly replied that he would respect Vienna’s approach. But Wilhelm refused to receive Szögyény.

choices.text: Bow to Berlin and harden the demands: add Austrian officials to the investigation and attach a 48-hour deadline
choices.why: Losing Berlin is worse than the risk of war
choices.after: The strengthened note was delivered in Belgrade with a 48-hour deadline. Serbia prepared a reply much like the one it actually gave, accepting most points but rejecting any part for Austrian officials in the investigation.

note.text: Behind the German leaders' haste in July 1914 lay a calculation that Russia’s “Great Programme” and France’s Three-Year Law (1913) would leave Germany militarily outmatched within a few years.

AT-06M.title: Serbia’s Answer
AT-06M.scene: Serbia has accepted almost every point of the note. Pašić promised to dissolve the anti-Austrian societies and investigate those involved, asking only that the detailed procedure for the inquiry be agreed on. Russia was relieved, and London praised Vienna’s restraint. But Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, the leader of the Black Hand, is still chief of Serbian military intelligence.

voices.text: Serbia has accepted, but no one has touched the officers who actually handed over the weapons. Without a way to monitor the promises, this victory will not last more than a few months.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: In 1909, too, Serbia promised to be a good neighbor. Without an army on the frontier, promises are waste paper.

choices.text: Accept the reply and declare a diplomatic victory. Leave monitoring to an international commission set up by the powers.
choices.why: A victory won without bloodshed is worth securing
choices.after: Half of Vienna’s papers spoke of victory, the other half of humiliation. Tisza told the Hungarian parliament it was a victory won without bloodshed.

choices.text: Demand more, as Giesl warns: make it a condition that Apis and the officers who supplied the weapons be handed over
choices.why: Promises mean nothing while those responsible stay in place
