choices.after: Serbia insisted it could not hand its chief of military intelligence to a foreign power. In the end a compromise was reached under which Apis retired from active service, but in Serbia it remained one more humiliation.

choices.text: Accept the reply, but send officials to monitor compliance and treat any violation as grounds for military action
choices.why: Bank the pretext now and strike when the time comes
choices.after: Vienna announced that it accepted the reply, but the officials sent to Belgrade began recording Serbia’s compliance point by point. Conrad, the Chief of the General Staff, is waiting for the day the first violation is reported.

note.text: Apis was in fact sentenced to death on other charges at the Salonika trial held by the Serbian government in exile in 1917, and executed. During the proceedings he stated that he had organized the Sarajevo assassination.

AT-06Ma.place: Vienna, Foreign Ministry, Ballhausplatz (Joint Council of Ministers)
AT-06Ma.title: Memories of the Pig War
AT-06Ma.scene: Now that Serbia has accepted Vienna’s demands, the Joint Council discusses what comes next. In 1906 the Hungarian government banned imports of Serbian livestock, citing disease, and started a tariff war, the so-called Pig War, during which Serbia held out by finding new markets such as Germany and building meatpacking plants. During the Balkan War of 1912 you yourself considered a plan to bind Serbia to the empire through economic cooperation such as a customs union. Reopening the market to Serbia would reward its cooperation, but Hungary’s landowners and farmers have no wish to see cheap Serbian livestock come in.

voices.text: We cannot hand the Hungarian farmer’s market to Serbian pigs. Railways and transit trade are compensation enough.

voices.who: Report of the Foreign Ministry’s commercial department (gist)
voices.text: After the tariff war, Serbia’s trade shifted toward Germany and Salonika. The longer the market stays closed, the more Belgrade leans on countries other than Vienna.

choices.text: Reopen the market as the commercial report advises, trading livestock quotas and transit trade for Serbia’s cooperation
choices.why: Open the market and Serbia will lean on Vienna
choices.after: Tisza agreed reluctantly after cutting the quotas, and the agrarian deputies in the Hungarian parliament attacked the government fiercely. In Belgrade, Pašić held up the agreement as an achievement in the election campaign.

choices.text: Keep the livestock market closed, as Tisza wishes, and keep up economic pressure until Serbia honors every promise
choices.why: Ease the pressure and Serbia will break its word
choices.after: Serbia’s exports kept flowing toward Salonika and Germany. Vienna’s papers praised the firmness, but in Belgrade any politician who sought closer ties with Vienna was still branded a toady.

note.text: By some estimates, Austria-Hungary bought about 88 percent of Serbia’s exports before the tariff war, but afterward its share of Serbia’s foreign trade fell to around 30 percent. The dispute was halted for a time by a commercial treaty in 1908, but ratification was delayed by the annexation crisis, and some works date its end to 1909 or 1911.

AT-07M.title: Conrad’s Resignation
AT-07M.scene: Conrad has submitted his resignation to the Emperor. He was dismissed once in 1911 for urging a preventive war against Italy and became Chief of the General Staff again during the Balkan crisis of 1912. Ironically, the man who had most firmly blocked his calls for preventive war was Archduke Franz Ferdinand, killed at Sarajevo. Now the army has lost its patron, and the officer corps says the diplomats have marched it up and down for nothing for the third time.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: In three years Russia will have finished rearming. If we fight then, the empire cannot win. I cannot take responsibility for that defeat.
Preventive war does not save the empire; it gambles with the empire’s life. Give the army a budget instead of a war.

choices.text: Accept the resignation. Remove the advocate of preventive war and appoint a cautious general who respects diplomacy.
choices.why: Let soldiers set policy and the crises will keep returning
choices.after: Conrad left for the mountains of Tyrol. In Berlin, Moltke sent Vienna’s new Chief of the General Staff a polite but cold letter.

choices.text: Refuse Conrad’s resignation. Put a budget for artillery and more troops before both parliaments to soothe the army.
choices.why: Placate the army now to be ready for the next crisis
choices.after: The Emperor handed back the resignation, and both parliaments passed the budget for artillery and more troops. Conrad settled down to wait for the next crisis.

note.text: Conrad repeatedly urged a preventive war against Italy in 1911, lost the Emperor’s confidence and was dismissed, then returned as Chief of the General Staff in December 1912 amid the tensions of the Balkan War.

AT-08M.title: After the Old Emperor
AT-08M.scene: On 21 November 1916, the same day he died in fact, Franz Joseph dies at Schönbrunn, aged eighty-six. With the Emperor of 68 years gone, Czechs, South Slavs and Romanians press their demands for autonomy all at once. Russia’s “Great Programme” is close to completion, and border disputes have flared up again in the Balkans. The young new Emperor, Karl, asks you for your last advice.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (former Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: We should have struck in 1914. Even now we must strike before Russia finishes its preparations.
What protects the empire is order, not war. A pact with Russia fixing the Balkan boundaries costs less than a war.

choices.text: Make a Balkan pact with Russia, as Tisza says, placing the Serbian and Bulgarian questions under great-power guarantee
choices.why: Order, not war, is what protects the empire
choices.after: The foreign ministers of Vienna and St Petersburg sat down together over the Balkans. Whether the mistrust that began at Buchlau in 1908 can be cleared away depends on how much patience the hard-liners in both empires show.

choices.text: Strike first with Germany, as Conrad says, before Russia’s Great Programme is complete. Any later and we cannot win.
choices.why: With every year that passes, only Russia grows stronger
choices.after: The war put off in 1914 began on a larger scale, and this time Russia, too, was ready.

note.text: Franz Joseph reigned for 68 years, from 1848 to 1916. He did not live to see the end of the war, and his successor, Karl I, saw the empire dissolve within two years.

AT-08N.title: Time for Negotiation
AT-08N.scene: When Vienna turned to negotiation, telegrams of relief flowed in from London and St Petersburg. But partial mobilization against Serbia is already under way, and Russia has entered its “Period Preparatory to War.” In Berlin, Moltke warns that the longer the talks drag on, the more time Russia gains, while in Vienna Conrad has laid his resignation on his desk. What to do with the army while the talks go on has become as important as the talks themselves.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Stop mobilizing and, as in 1912, we will have spent the money and broken the army’s morale. Negotiate if you must, but the army must be kept ready to the end.
The Hungarian parliament will gladly accept a result won by negotiation. But one step on the Russian frontier and everything collapses.

choices.text: Pledge, as Tisza says, that there will be no military measures on the Russian frontier while talks are under way
choices.why: Talks survive only if Russia is not provoked
choices.after: Russia slowed its preparations for partial mobilization. Moltke made no secret of his annoyance that Vienna was leaving Germany’s back exposed.

choices.text: Keep mobilizing to the end, as Conrad says. Negotiate, but do not slow the army’s preparations.
choices.why: You must be ready in case the talks break down
choices.after: The conference room and the parade ground were busy at the same time. The Russian General Staff reported to the Tsar that Austria was playing for time while preparing for war.

choices.text: Break off the talks and declare war on Serbia, creating a fait accompli before more mediation proposals pile up
choices.why: The longer the talks last, the longer the empire sits in the dock
choices.after: The telegram declaring war reached the Serbian government at Niš by way of Romania. With the hopes pinned on negotiation dashed, London and St Petersburg hardened even faster than they did in fact.

note.text: During the Balkan War, in the winter of 1912, Austria-Hungary built up large forces on the Russian and Serbian frontiers and then stood them down without fighting. This costly episode became the army’s argument in 1914 that this time it must go all the way.

AT-08Na.title: Berlin’s Timetable
AT-08Na.clock: 2 days until the London ambassadors' conference
AT-08Na.scene: Three days have passed since Vienna turned to negotiation. Russian and Austrian preparations for mobilization have not stopped, and in Berlin the Chief of the General Staff, Moltke, urges that Germany too must mobilize before Russia gets ahead. Germany’s war plan requires that, in a war with Russia, France be struck first, so the moment Berlin moves, these talks become a question of the western frontier. Two days remain before the ambassadors' conference meets in London.

voices.text: If Russia moves to general mobilization, Germany cannot wait. If Vienna is negotiating, it must get Russia to stop mobilizing as well.
If Germany moves its army west, these talks lose their meaning. We must ask Berlin for time.

choices.text: Make a formal request to Berlin, as Tisza says: send no ultimatum to Russia until the negotiations are over
choices.why: Stop Germany’s timetable before it wrecks the talks
choices.after: Bethmann Hollweg replied that he would wait one more day, on condition that Russia stopped mobilizing. Moltke snapped back: did they know what that one day meant on the western front?

choices.text: Leave Germany’s decisions to Germany, and carry on with both the London talks and your own mobilization
choices.why: Better not to meddle in your ally’s decisions
choices.after: Berlin drafted a telegram demanding that Russia demobilize. Before the ambassadors could even gather in London, the timetables outside the conference room had begun to move.

note.text: In 1914 Germany delivered a 12-hour ultimatum to Russia on 31 July, declared war on 1 August and that same evening sent troops into Luxembourg.

AT-09N.title: What Is to Be Done with Serbia?
AT-09N.scene: The great powers' ambassadors are seated around a round table. The issue is who should take part, and in what capacity, in investigating those behind the Sarajevo assassination. Serbia insists that foreign officials taking part in an investigation on its soil would violate its sovereignty, while Vienna says Serbia’s own investigation cannot be trusted. The Russian ambassador defends Serbia and the German ambassador defends Austria, but both want above all to avoid war.

voices.text: Grey says he will recognize Vienna’s legitimate demands. But no country will support a clause that strikes directly at Serbia’s sovereignty.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: A promise without a pledge becomes waste paper, like Serbia’s good-neighbor declaration of 1909. Unless we hold Belgrade, nothing will change.

choices.text: Accept the plan Mensdorff reports: an international commission led by neutral jurists, with Austrian officials as observers
choices.why: Respect sovereignty and the powers will side with the empire
choices.after: The international commission set off for Belgrade. Vienna’s hard-line papers called it a humiliation, but Europe’s trains carried summer holidaymakers instead of soldiers.

choices.text: Make a pledge occupation of Belgrade the condition, as Conrad says, and withdraw once Serbia keeps its promises
choices.why: Without a pledge, promises become waste paper
choices.after: The ambassadors' conference reluctantly accepted the Austrian army’s entry into Belgrade. Russia protested but did not move its army, and the soldiers who had crossed the Sava halted in Belgrade.

note.text: On 31 March 1909 Serbia accepted the annexation of Bosnia and declared that it would maintain good-neighborly relations with Austria-Hungary. In its 1914 ultimatum Vienna accused Serbia of breaking this promise.

AT-10H.title: A Pledge Occupation
AT-10H.event: On the afternoon of 30 July Nicholas II again approved general mobilization. In Berlin, Moltke says Germany cannot simply stand by and watch Russia mobilize.
AT-10H.scene: In Berlin, Bethmann Hollweg was relieved at the news that Vienna had accepted the “Halt in Belgrade.” But Russian general mobilization has already begun, and the German General Staff grows more anxious with every day of delay. The Austrian army is ready to cross the Sava and enter Belgrade, and Conrad insists that unless Russia stands down, troops must be sent to Galicia as well. If the Tsar is to stop mobilizing, he needs something that lets him save face.

voices.text: Sazonov wants a written commitment that Austria will respect Serbian sovereignty. Only then, he says, can he persuade the Tsar.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Russia is only buying time. Slow our mobilization and we hand them Galicia for nothing.

choices.text: Take Szápáry’s advice and pledge in writing to Russia: no annexation, respect for Serbian sovereignty, a time limit on occupation
choices.why: The Tsar must be given grounds to step back
choices.after: The written pledge went to St Petersburg that night. The Tsar replied that he would halt mobilization but not reverse it, and now every country waits for the conference in London.

choices.text: As Conrad says, answer general mobilization with general mobilization: occupy Belgrade, but send troops to Galicia too
choices.why: Watch Russia mobilize and do nothing, and you lose Galicia
choices.after: The Emperor signed the order for general mobilization. The promise to stop at Belgrade still stood, but the Russian and German mobilization timetables had already gone too far to be stopped.

note.text: In the Bosnian annexation crisis of March 1909, Russia backed down under German pressure, and Serbia declared that it would keep good-neighborly relations with Austria. It was one reason why Russia’s leaders in 1914 resolved never to back down again.

AT-11H.place: London ambassadors' conference / Foreign Ministry, Vienna
AT-11H.title: From Belgrade to the Conference Table
AT-11H.scene: The Austrian army has entered Belgrade and halted. The Serbian government, now at Niš, has not given up its will to resist, and in London the great powers' ambassadors have gathered to decide how Serbia is to be dealt with. Russia has stopped mobilizing but not stood down, and the German and French armies wait on their frontiers. In the conference room, the Austrian ambassador, Mensdorff, awaits his instructions from Vienna.

voices.text: The longer we hold Belgrade, the more hostile Serbs the empire takes on. We must get our promises and get out quickly.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Withdraw and Serbia will be back on its feet within a few years. The pledge must be held to the end.

choices.text: As Tisza says, withdraw from Belgrade in stages, provided an international mission oversees Serbia’s investigation
choices.why: The longer the occupation, the more hostile the population
choices.after: Serbia accepted investigation and punishment under great-power supervision, and over several months the Austrian army returned north of the Sava. Conrad openly vented his frustration at what he called a half victory.

choices.text: As Conrad says, keep holding Belgrade until Serbia has carried out every last one of the demands
choices.why: Give up the pledge and Serbia will rise again
choices.after: A military government was set up in Belgrade. In Russia anger boiled over at the Slav brothers' being abandoned once again, and the army, still mobilized, stood on the frontier.

note.text: During the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913, too, the great powers' ambassadors met in London and drew borders. The ambassadors' conference was then a device that kept the great powers from going to war with one another, but in July 1914 Vienna saw it as a place where Austria would be put in the dock.

SL-01.title: The Archduke’s Vision
SL-01.event: On 1 July Tisza sent the Emperor a memorandum warning that using Sarajevo as a pretext to strike Serbia, without evidence, would be a fatal mistake.
SL-01.scene: You have rejected Conrad’s demands and taken up again the course Franz Ferdinand spoke of while he lived. The Archduke regarded the dualist system of 1867 as a disaster and believed that if the empire’s Slavs were treated fairly, the separatist movements would fade. During the Balkan War of 1912 you yourself considered a plan to draw Serbia to the empire through economic cooperation such as a customs union. But the key to this course lies with the Hungarian prime minister, Tisza, who long clashed with the Archduke over policy toward the nationalities of the Kingdom of Hungary.

voices.text: I agree that war should be avoided. But the Hungarian parliament will not accept new rights for the Slavs of the Kingdom of Hungary, or a market opened to Serbian livestock.
Offer markets and railways to the country that killed the Archduke, and Europe will read it as weakness. In 1909, too, Belgrade made promises and did not keep them.

choices.text: Revive the customs union idea of 1912: offer a trade treaty and transit trade for Serbia’s help with the inquiry
choices.why: Economic pull lasts longer than the bayonet
choices.after: The Foreign Ministry’s commercial department got out the files on the 1912 customs union idea again. In Budapest the agrarian associations, on rumor alone, stirred at the prospect of Serbian pigs coming back.

choices.text: Start at home: investigate the riot damage in Sarajevo and Zagreb and protect the empire’s loyal Serb subjects
choices.why: Win over the empire’s own Serbs before anything else
choices.after: When a statement in the Emperor’s name ordered an inquiry into the riot damage, the Croat-Serb Coalition in Zagreb welcomed it. But Potiorek, the governor of Bosnia, and the soldiers in Vienna protested that it amounted to shielding the Serbs.

note.text: According to Valiani, Franz Ferdinand wrote to Berchtold on 1 February 1913 opposing war with Serbia and saying that if the empire’s Slavs enjoyed a fair and comfortable life, the separatist movements would soon cease. In a character sketch written ten years after the Archduke’s death, Berchtold recalled that had he come to the throne, he would have tried to turn the dualist system into a supranational federation.

SL-02.place: Vienna, Foreign Ministry, Ballhausplatz (Joint Council of Ministers)
SL-02.title: Tisza’s Line
SL-02.scene: On the table of the Joint Council lies not a war plan but a set of proposals for Serbia. The Austrian prime minister Stürgkh, the war minister Krobatin and the joint finance minister Biliński, who is responsible for Bosnia, object that the army and Bosnia will read the proposals as weakness. Tisza has taken your side in avoiding war, but where the Slavs of the Kingdom of Hungary and Hungarian agriculture are at stake, he will not yield an inch. Berlin has been told that Vienna has chosen a diplomatic solution, and Ambassador Tschirschky is reporting that Vienna once again cannot make up its mind.

voices.text: The Serb understands only force. Open the market to them and the Serbs of Bosnia will think Vienna has lost its nerve.
I can open the way to railways and transit trade for Serbia. But do not expect the Hungarian parliament to accept livestock imports or South Slav autonomy.

choices.text: Accept Tisza’s line: no livestock market; offer Serbia only railways, transit trade and cooperation on the inquiry
choices.why: Without Hungary’s consent, any proposal will collapse
choices.after: The proposal shrank, but Tisza promised to defend at least this much in the Hungarian parliament. Biliński and Krobatin had their dissent entered in the minutes.

choices.text: Go over Tisza’s head: ask the Emperor directly for Hungarian concessions and open the market even to Serbian livestock
choices.why: A half-measure will never move Belgrade to act
choices.after: The Emperor did not want a head-on clash with the Hungarian prime minister, and Tisza spoke of resigning. The livestock market survived only as a phrase, “to be discussed later,” and the Budapest papers wrote that the foreign minister had tried to sell out the Hungarian farmer.

note.text: In 1906 the Hungarian government banned imports of Serbian livestock, citing disease, and so began the so-called Pig War. Behind it lay Serbia’s efforts to escape Vienna’s economic sway by buying French guns and forming a customs union with Bulgaria; in the end Vienna failed to bring Belgrade to heel through economic pressure.

SL-03.title: Between Berlin and Belgrade

telegram.text: Ambassador Szögyény / German Foreign Office disappointed by Vienna’s proposal to Serbia / mood that Austria-Hungary can hardly be relied on if this chance is missed

SL-03.event: On the evening of 10 July Hartwig, the Russian minister to Serbia, collapsed with a heart attack and died while talking with Giesl at the Austrian legation in Belgrade.
SL-03.scene: The proposal has not yet gone to Belgrade. Haymerle, the counselor at the embassy in Berlin, writes that the German Foreign Office is pressing for action from all sides, and Conrad is ready to brandish his resignation, saying the army is being marched up and down for nothing again. In Belgrade, Pašić, out campaigning for the elections, risks attack from the Black Hand and the nationalist press if he gives even the impression of joining hands with Vienna. You must decide whether to send the proposal, or withdraw it and return to a hard-line ultimatum.

voices.who: Hoyos (the foreign minister’s chef de cabinet)
voices.text: Lose Berlin and the empire stands alone against Russia. Even if you send the proposal, attach a deadline and a pledge to it.
Push Pašić publicly and he cannot back down. Send it through a quiet channel and leave him something he can show at home.

choices.text: Send the proposal quietly, as Giesl advises: open trade and railways, and ask for help investigating those involved
choices.why: Pašić must be left something to show at home
choices.after: Giesl took the proposal to the Serbian Foreign Ministry. London and Rome were surprised by Vienna’s approach but welcomed it, while in Berlin Jagow complained that Vienna was putting its own calculations ahead of the alliance.

choices.text: Withdraw the proposal, as Conrad and Berlin wish. Put Musulin to work on a hard-line ultimatum instead.
choices.why: Lose Berlin and the empire is left alone
choices.after: You put the proposal in a drawer and gave the drafting of the ultimatum to Musulin, the diplomat from Croatia. Once again the Archduke’s vision never got beyond the council rooms of Vienna, and Tisza again made it his condition that no Serbian territory be annexed.

note.text: Hartwig had been in Belgrade since 1909, was close to the Pašić government and was regarded as the architect of the Balkan League of 1912. Yet in 1912 the Russian government did not back Serbia’s push into Albania, so Belgrade and St Petersburg did not always want the same things.

PA-01.place: Vienna, Foreign Ministry, Ballhausplatz (Joint Council of Ministers)
PA-01.title: The Sword Stays Sheathed
PA-01.scene: Hoyos did not go to Berlin, and on the table of the Joint Council lies not a blank check but the draft of a diplomatic note. Tisza has sided with you for the first time, but Krobatin and Biliński sit stony-faced, warning that the Serbs of Bosnia will hold the empire in contempt. The German ambassador in Vienna, Tschirschky, hints that the Kaiser in Berlin expects resolve from Vienna. Around this time, in fact, Wilhelm wrote in the margin of a cautious report from Tschirschky: “Now or never.”

voices.text: A diplomatic success will be read as weakness by the army and in Bosnia. Send only a note and the next assassin will be bolder.
Europe must first see that Serbia has failed in its duty as an honest neighbor. Then, even if war becomes necessary, the empire will not be the aggressor.

choices.text: As Tisza says, compile a dossier showing Serbia’s guilt, circulate it to the powers, and demand a joint inquiry
choices.why: Win the argument in front of Europe before anything else
choices.after: Wiesner, the Foreign Ministry’s legal adviser, left for Sarajevo to gather the investigation records. Vienna did in fact prepare a dossier for the powers in 1914, but as a way to build the case for war.

choices.text: Inform Berlin, but ask it to back diplomatic pressure rather than war, putting Germany’s weight behind the talks
choices.why: An ally’s strength is worth more as pressure than in war
choices.after: Bethmann Hollweg replied that he would respect Vienna’s caution. But Szögyény reported that Wilhelm had grumbled about another chance thrown away.

note.text: From 4 July the Foreign Ministry in Vienna ran a committee to gather material proving Serbia’s guilt; inside the ministry it was called the “war factory.”

PA-02.title: Pašić’s Answer

telegram.text: Minister Giesl / reply of Prime Minister Pašić / promises investigation and punishment of those involved on Serbian territory / participation of foreign officials in investigation constitutionally impossible / willing to report results

PA-02.scene: Pašić, in the middle of his election campaign, has sent a polite but watertight answer. Serbia will investigate and punish those involved on its own territory, but cannot accept foreign officials taking part in an investigation inside Serbia. The Serbian government did in fact learn early on who had handed over the weapons used in the plot, but could not touch Apis, the head of military intelligence. How this answer is received will decide whether the investigation brings out the truth or ends as a delaying tactic.

voices.text: Serbia’s own investigation will be as hollow as its good-neighbor promise of 1909. Who would believe the Belgrade police investigating military intelligence?
Pašić counts on Russian support, but he does not want war. Give him a way out that saves face and you may gain a surprising amount.

choices.text: Propose an international commission led by neutral jurists, with Austrian officials taking part only as observers
choices.why: This answers both Serbian sovereignty and the empire’s suspicions
choices.after: After two days of deliberation Pašić accepted the international commission. London and Paris judged Vienna’s proposal reasonable.

choices.text: Give Pašić a way out, as Giesl advises: accept Serbia’s own investigation and verify only the results
choices.why: Let him save face and you can get more out of him
choices.after: The Belgrade police arrested a few minor officials. Vienna’s hard-liners sneered that the investigation was a sham.

note.text: Serbia faced elections in August 1914, and the Pašić government was locked in a power struggle with the Black Hand, the army’s secret society. That is why Pašić could not lightly move against military intelligence.

PA-02a.title: Tankosić and Ciganović
PA-02a.scene: The Serbian investigation has quickly turned up two names: Milan Ciganović, a railway employee who gave the assassins bombs and pistols, and the man behind him, Major Vojislav Tankosić. Tankosić is close to Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, the leader of the Black Hand. After a struggle between the army and the government in the spring of 1914, King Peter I on 24 June made his son Alexander regent and handed him the royal powers, and Pašić, facing elections, is in no position to move lightly against the army.

voices.text: Pašić knew both men. The question is whether he can stand up to Apis.
Demand their arrest, but give him a generous deadline. If Pašić falls, the soldiers will take his place.

choices.text: Set a ten-day deadline and tell Belgrade, through Giesl, to arrest both men and put them on trial
choices.why: Without a deadline, the investigation will drag on forever
choices.after: Pašić arrested Tankosić, but Ciganović had already gone into hiding. Vienna’s hard-liners called it half-compliance, and officers in Belgrade muttered that Pašić had given in to foreign demands.

choices.text: Give Pašić time, as Tisza says, and settle for his promise to deal with the army after the elections
choices.why: If Pašić falls, the soldiers will seize power
choices.after: Through unofficial channels Pašić let it be known that after the elections he would deal with military intelligence. But Vienna’s papers wrote that the men who supplied the weapons that killed the Archduke were walking freely in the streets of Belgrade.

note.text: In 1914 Belgrade knew early on who had procured the weapons, but Tankosić was arrested only after the ultimatum was delivered on 23 July, and Ciganović slipped away.

PA-03.title: A Chill from Berlin
PA-03.scene: Now that the crisis has subsided, Berlin has cooled. German diplomats whisper that Austria has once again failed to act, and ask whether there is any reason to cling to a useless ally. London and St Petersburg, by contrast, praise Vienna’s restraint and offer to work with it on the Balkan question. You must decide whether to win back Germany’s trust or to open a separate line of talks with the Entente as well.

voices.text: The Kaiser believes Vienna has thrown away its chance. Unless we show the value of the alliance again, Berlin will look for another path.
Grey considers that the empire acted as a responsible great power in the Balkans. This time Britain will listen to Vienna.

choices.text: Heed Szögyény’s warning: hold staff talks with Germany to reaffirm the alliance, and raise the rearmament budget
choices.why: Lose Germany’s trust and the empire is left alone
choices.after: Conrad and Moltke met again. The two chiefs of staff agreed that in the next crisis there would be no hesitation.

choices.text: As Mensdorff proposes, keep the alliance but open a separate channel with Britain to discuss the Balkans
choices.why: It is safer not to rely on a single alliance
choices.after: Talks on the Balkans began between Vienna and London. In Berlin, Jagow suspected that Vienna was trying to make friends with others behind Germany’s back.

note.text: For Germany in 1914, Austria-Hungary was the only reliable ally. Italy was a member of the Triple Alliance, but it declared neutrality in August 1914 and entered the war on the Entente side in May 1915.

PA-04.title: Conrad’s Resignation
PA-04.scene: Conrad, the Chief of the General Staff, has handed the Emperor his resignation. In 1913 alone he called for war with Serbia more than twenty times, and the man who had most firmly blocked his calls for preventive war was Archduke Franz Ferdinand, killed at Sarajevo. The army, having lost its patron, says the diplomats have humiliated it once again. You must decide whether to keep him or let him go.

voices.who: Conrad von Hötzendorf (Chief of the General Staff)
voices.text: Russia will have finished rearming by 1917. If we do not fight before then, the empire will lose even the chance to fight.
A country where the Chief of the General Staff makes policy does not last. Give the army a budget instead of a war.

choices.text: Accept Conrad’s resignation, as Tisza says. Remove the advocate of preventive war and let the Foreign Ministry set policy.
choices.why: A state where the chief of staff makes policy will not last
choices.after: Conrad took off his uniform and left for Tyrol. Vienna’s hard-line papers wrote that the empire had lost its last general.

choices.text: Refuse Conrad’s resignation. Placate the army with a rearmament budget and prepare for the next crisis.
choices.why: Build up the army now to weather the next crisis
choices.after: The Emperor handed back the resignation. Both parliaments passed the budget for artillery and more troops, and Conrad settled down to wait for the next crisis.

note.text: The historian Hew Strachan counts 25 occasions on which Conrad called for war with Serbia in the year from January 1913 to January 1914.

PA-05.title: The South Slav Question
PA-05.scene: Having avoided war, the empire now faces its problems at home. South Slav politicians in Croatia and Bosnia say they have been treated with suspicion since Sarajevo and demand autonomy free of Hungarian interference. While he lived, Archduke Franz Ferdinand showed interest in plans to remake the empire as a federation of its peoples, but the greatest opponent of such plans was Hungary. Reform could save the empire, or it could bring down the Compromise of 1867.

voices.text: The moment the South Slavs are given autonomy, the Kingdom of Hungary will break apart. The Compromise of 1867 is a pillar of the empire that cannot be touched.

voices.who: Hoyos (the foreign minister’s chef de cabinet)
voices.text: If we cannot satisfy the South Slavs within the empire, they will look to Belgrade. The way to defeat Serbia is to reform the empire.

choices.text: Push for reforms widening South Slav autonomy, as Hoyos says, and accept the backlash from Hungary
choices.why: Only a reformed empire can prevail against Serbia
choices.after: Cheers broke out in Zagreb and fury in Budapest. Tisza warned that the reform bill could not pass the Hungarian parliament.

choices.text: Uphold the Compromise of 1867, as Tisza says. Keep the South Slav status quo and avoid a quarrel with Hungary.
choices.why: Reform that shakes the empire’s pillars is more dangerous
choices.after: The Compromise of 1867 stayed as it was. Disappointed South Slav politicians quietly turned their eyes toward Belgrade.

note.text: Around 1910 Austria-Hungary had about 50 million people, and Germans and Magyars together made up less than half. The rest were Czechs, Poles, Ukrainians (Ruthenians), Romanians, Croats, Serbs, Slovaks, Slovenes, Italians and others.

PA-05a.title: Budapest’s Veto
PA-05a.scene: Budapest has answered Vienna’s moves on the South Slav question. From the rostrum of the Hungarian parliament, Tisza declares that no reform can alter the Compromise of 1867 or the territory of the Kingdom of Hungary. Croatia-Slavonia already belongs to the Hungarian crown, and Vienna and Budapest have long quarreled over which side Bosnia should be attached to. Since the death of Franz Ferdinand, who wanted to end the dualist system, hardly anyone but you and the young heir, Karl, is left to back this reform.

voices.text: If a decree is issued carving a South Slav state out of the lands of the Kingdom of Hungary, the Hungarian government will not last a single day.

voices.who: Hoyos (the foreign minister’s chef de cabinet)
voices.text: Unless Bosnia and Croatia are united and the South Slavs given their due share, they will keep looking to Belgrade.

choices.text: Compromise with Tisza: attach Bosnia to Croatia-Slavonia, but keep it under the Hungarian crown
choices.why: Better to reform only as far as Hungary will accept
choices.after: Tisza was satisfied that Bosnia would come to the Hungarian side, and the Coalition in Zagreb welcomed the enlargement of Croatian lands. But it was not a reform that gave the South Slavs a place equal to Vienna and Budapest, and the Serbs of Bosnia were disappointed.

choices.text: As Hoyos says, ask the Emperor for a decree making a South Slav kingdom the third pillar, and take on Hungary
choices.why: Half a reform cannot hold the South Slavs
choices.after: In the end the Emperor did not sign. The old monarch who had sent troops to dissolve the Hungarian parliament in 1906 had no wish to clash head-on with Budapest again, and the reform plan went into a drawer.

note.text: In 1906 Aurel Popovici, a Romanian jurist among the scholars around Franz Ferdinand, proposed a “United States of Greater Austria” dividing the empire into 15 states along national lines. The Archduke himself wanted to end dualism and move toward a stronger federal system, but by 1914 there had been almost no progress on reforming the empire.

PA-06.title: After the Old Emperor: The Last Choice
PA-06.scene: On 21 November 1916, the same day he died in fact, Franz Joseph dies at Schönbrunn, aged eighty-six. With the Emperor who held the empire together for 68 years gone, border disputes break out again in the Balkans, and Russia’s “Great Programme” is close to completion. The young new Emperor, Karl, does not want war, but the army says this is the last chance. You must now make the decision that was put off in the summer of 1914.

voices.text: We should have struck in 1914. Even now we must strike, together with Germany, before Russia finishes its preparations.
What the old Emperor preserved was peace. The new Emperor’s first decision must not be war.

choices.text: As Tisza says, agree Balkan spheres of influence with Russia and settle border disputes at a great-power conference
choices.why: The new Emperor’s first decision must be for peace
choices.after: The ambassadors of Vienna and St Petersburg began negotiating the Balkan question in London. But the moment the pact was signed, the two empires' general staffs began revising their plans for the next war.

choices.text: As Conrad says, strike first with Germany before Russia’s Great Programme is complete. Any later and the chance is gone.
choices.why: The last chance comes before Russia finishes preparing
choices.after: The war put off in 1914 began on a larger scale, and this time Russia, too, was ready.

note.text: Karl I, who came to the throne in 1916, did in fact attempt secret peace talks with France in 1917 through his brother-in-law, Prince Sixtus, but failed, and when the affair came to light it badly shook relations with Germany.

epilogues.A: Berchtold would have gone down as the foreign minister who prevented war, but the army in Vienna and the hard-line press would have attacked him to the end as the aristocrat who papered over the Archduke’s death with a few diplomatic documents. Tisza would have claimed the bloodless victory as his own and gained still more power in Budapest, while Conrad remained an advocate of preventive war, waiting for the next crisis. Yet the Czechs, South Slavs and Romanians would still have demanded autonomy, and Franz Joseph in fact died in November 1916. Whether a multinational empire without its old Emperor could have reformed itself in peace, no one can know.
epilogues.B: Holding Belgrade as a pledge, the Austrian army made Serbia carry out its promises, and Vienna seemed to have won its first clear victory in the Balkans since the annexation crisis of 1908. Conrad made no secret of his discontent at a half victory, while Tisza, having secured victory without annexation, would have enjoyed firmer support in Hungary. But Russia did not forget the humiliation of backing down a second time after 1909, and South Slav nationalism did not vanish with the occupation of Belgrade. No one in St Petersburg would have believed that the Tsar would back down again in the next crisis.
epilogues.E: Austria-Hungary’s war of 1914 went wrong from the start. In August the Serbian army threw back the invaders at Cer, and in the battles of Galicia the empire lost Lemberg (today Lviv in Ukraine), with more than 300,000 men killed, wounded or captured. Among them was Conrad’s son Herbert. Berchtold, who considered territorial concessions to keep Italy out of the war, resigned in January 1915 and died on his Hungarian estate in 1942. Conrad married Gina in 1915 and in March 1917 was removed as Chief of the General Staff by the new Emperor, Karl. Tisza, who backed the war to the end, was murdered at his home in Budapest on 31 October 1918 by armed men in uniform. Around the same time Czechoslovakia and a South Slav state declared independence, and when Emperor Karl withdrew from affairs of state in November 1918, the Habsburg empire, centuries old, vanished from the map. Andrian-Werburg, a diplomat who had been at the Foreign Ministry in July 1914, later wrote: “We have started this war, not the Germans, and still less the Entente – that much I know.”
epilogues.F: Having come through the summer of 1914, the empire bought a few years, but those were also the years in which Russia’s “Great Programme” was completed. After the old Emperor’s death, Vienna drew the sword first in a new Balkan crisis, and this time it faced a Russia that was ready. The preventive war Conrad had demanded all his life came at last, but the favorable moment he had spoken of was long gone. Even a decision that keeps the peace may, depending on the choices that follow, do no more than buy time.

dossier.t: Born in Vienna on 18 April 1863, you are 51 in July 1914. You grew up at Buchlau Castle in Moravia, learning Czech, Slovak and Hungarian, and are known as one of the richest men in Austria-Hungary. In 1893 you married Ferdinandine, of the great Hungarian Károlyi family. After postings in Paris and London you served as ambassador in St Petersburg from 1906 to 1911, and in 1908 you hosted the secret meeting between Aehrenthal and Izvolsky at your castle. When Aehrenthal died in February 1912 you succeeded him, reportedly against your own inclination; at 49 you were the youngest foreign minister in Europe.

Your chef de cabinet, Count Hoyos, is the man who went to Berlin during the annexation crisis of 1908 and came back with Germany’s support. Count Forgách, a section chief, was minister in Belgrade from 1907 to 1911, lost face over the forged documents in the Friedjung trial and was moved to Dresden; he returned to the Foreign Ministry in the autumn of 1913. Haymerle, a counselor at the embassy in Berlin, wrote that when Forgách wanted something very much, the minister and Tisza would end up doing it. Baron Musulin, who polished the text of the ultimatum, is a diplomat from Croatia. The historian Rauchensteiner observes that all of these men built their careers on Russia, Serbia and the Balkans, lived through the annexation crisis, and this time meant to repeat what they had done then, without mistakes.

The Balkan Wars left you with a reputation as a weak and indecisive foreign minister. Rauchensteiner interprets it this way: because you were still optimistic in June 1914 that an agreement with Serbia was possible, after Sarajevo you felt that you had failed and been humiliated, and this time you did not want to look weak. At the meeting of 7 July you said that the Greater Serbian propaganda coming out of Belgrade was eating away at the empire as far as Zagreb and Zadar. Your hope was to show Europe the shameful part Serbia had played and so keep the war confined to Serbia. Vienna’s diplomats put the chance of Russian intervention at less than even.

movers.intro: The hostility between Austria and Serbia hardened through Serbia’s change of dynasty in 1903, the tariff war of 1906, the annexation crisis and forgery trials of 1908–1909, and the Balkan Wars. Whether in 1914 the two countries were merely proxies of Germany and Russia, and which of Vienna and Berlin was leading the other, is a long-running debate. The main views are these.
views: Samuel R. Williamson: holds that the decisive decisions leading to war in the summer of 1914 were made not by Germany but by Austria-Hungary. Through the Balkan Wars, Vienna’s diplomacy became steadily more militarized, and the Habsburg leaders came to believe that only war with Serbia could settle the South Slav problem.

Manfried Rauchensteiner: holds that it was Austria-Hungary that deliberately started the war, with Germany leading the way whenever Vienna hesitated. He adds that Russia, too, bore no small share of responsibility for starting the war.

Fritz Fischer and the work that followed him: hold that Berlin pushed Vienna on with the blank check and its constant urging, and that Germany’s leaders saw the crisis as an opportunity for a larger war. Rauchensteiner, too, reads the remark about a “great decision” made by the Berlin journalist Naumann to Hoyos on 1 July as an early sign that Berlin had more than the Serbian question in mind.

Christopher Clark: holds that Vienna’s grievances against Serbia had a real basis, and that Serbia, too, was no proxy doing Russia’s bidding but a state pursuing its own aims. Rather than laying the blame for the war on one country, he explains it as the joint product of leaders in many countries who misread one another.
movers.note: Some studies, such as Sean McMeekin’s, stress that Russia used Serbia to pursue its interests in the Balkans and the Straits. On the other hand, Russia did not back Serbia’s demands to the end in 1909 or 1912, and in the spring of 1914 the government and the army’s secret society were fighting for power in Belgrade, so it is hard to see Serbia as a country moved by a single will either.
